chapters.title: Chapter 1 — General Remarks
paragraphs: Among the circumstances that make up the present state of human knowledge, few are more unlike what we might have expected, or tell us more about the backward state in which speculation on the most important subjects still lingers, than how little progress has been made in settling the controversy over the criterion of right and wrong. From the dawn of philosophy, the question of the _summum bonum_, or in other words the foundation of morality, has been counted the main problem of speculative thought. It has occupied the most gifted minds and divided them into sects and schools, which have waged vigorous war on one another. After more than two thousand years the same discussions continue, and philosophers are still ranged under the same contending banners. Neither thinkers nor mankind at large seem any nearer to unanimity on the subject than when the young Socrates listened to the old Protagoras and argued the theory of utilitarianism against the popular morality of the so-called sophist (if Plato's dialogue is based on a real conversation).

It is true that similar confusion and uncertainty, and in some cases similar disagreement, exist about the first principles of all the sciences, even mathematics, which is considered the most certain of them. Yet this does not greatly impair the trustworthiness of the conclusions of those sciences, and generally does not impair it at all. The explanation of this apparent anomaly is that the detailed doctrines of a science are not usually deduced from its so-called first principles, nor do they rest on them for their evidence. If they did, no science would be more precarious, or have conclusions less adequately made out, than algebra. Algebra draws none of its certainty from what are commonly taught to learners as its elements, since these, as laid down by some of its most eminent teachers, are as full of fictions as English law and of mysteries as theology. The truths that are finally accepted as the first principles of a science are really the last results of metaphysical analysis, carried out on the elementary notions the science works with. Their relation to the science is not that of foundations to a building but of roots to a tree, which can do their work equally well even if they are never dug down to and exposed to the light. But although in science the particular truths come before the general theory, we might expect the opposite in a practical art such as morals or legislation. All action is for the sake of some end, and it seems natural to suppose that rules of action must take their whole character and color from the end they serve. When we engage in a pursuit, a clear and precise conception of what we are pursuing would seem to be the first thing we need, not the last thing we can look forward to. One would think that a test of right and wrong must be the means of finding out what is right or wrong, and not a consequence of having already found it out.

Turning to the popular theory of a natural faculty, a sense or instinct that informs us of right and wrong, does not get us around the difficulty. For one thing, the existence of such a moral instinct is itself one of the matters in dispute. For another, those believers in it who have any claim to philosophy have been obliged to give up the idea that it discerns what is right or wrong in the particular case at hand, as our other senses discern the sight or sound that is actually present. According to all its interpreters who deserve the name of thinkers, our moral faculty supplies us only with the general principles of moral judgments. It is a branch of our reason, not of our sensitive faculty, and we must look to it for the abstract doctrines of morality, not for perception of morality in the concrete. The intuitive school of ethics, no less than what may be called the inductive school, insists on the necessity of general laws. Both agree that the morality of an individual action is not a question of direct perception but of applying a law to an individual case. To a great extent they also recognize the same moral laws, but they differ about the evidence for those laws and the source of their authority. According to the one opinion, the principles of morals are evident _à priori_, needing nothing to command assent except that the meaning of the terms be understood. According to the other doctrine, right and wrong, like truth and falsehood, are questions of observation and experience. But both hold equally that morality must be deduced from principles, and the intuitive school affirms as strongly as the inductive that there is a science of morals. Yet the intuitive thinkers seldom attempt to draw up a list of the _à priori_ principles that are to serve as the premises of the science. Still more rarely do they make any effort to reduce those various principles to one first principle, or common ground of obligation. They either assume the ordinary precepts of morals to have _à priori_ authority, or they lay down as the common groundwork of those maxims some generality that is much less obviously authoritative than the maxims themselves, and that has never succeeded in gaining popular acceptance. Yet if their pretensions are to be supported, there ought to be either one fundamental principle or law at the root of all morality, or, if there are several, a determinate order of precedence among them. And the one principle, or the rule for deciding between the various principles when they conflict, ought to be self-evident.

To ask how far the bad effects of this deficiency have been softened in practice, or how far the moral beliefs of mankind have been corrupted or made uncertain by the lack of any distinct recognition of an ultimate standard, would require a complete survey and criticism of past and present ethical doctrine. Yet it would be easy to show that these moral beliefs owe whatever steadiness or consistency they have reached mainly to the tacit influence of a standard that has not been recognized. The absence of an acknowledged first principle has made ethics not so much a guide as a consecration of men's actual sentiments. Still, men's sentiments, both of favor and of aversion, are greatly influenced by what they suppose to be the effects of things on their happiness. So the principle of utility, or the greatest happiness principle as Bentham later called it, has had a large share in forming the moral doctrines even of those who most scornfully reject its authority. Nor is there any school of thought that refuses to admit that the influence of actions on happiness is a most material and even predominant consideration in many of the details of morals, however unwilling it may be to acknowledge it as the fundamental principle of morality and the source of moral obligation. I might go much further and say that for all those _à priori_ moralists who think it necessary to argue at all, utilitarian arguments are indispensable. It is not my present purpose to criticize these thinkers, but I cannot help referring, by way of illustration, to a systematic treatise by one of the most illustrious of them, the _Metaphysics of Ethics_ by Kant. This remarkable man, whose system of thought will long remain one of the landmarks in the history of philosophical speculation, does in that treatise lay down a universal first principle as the origin and ground of moral obligation. It is this: "So act, that the rule on which thou actest would admit of being adopted as a law by all rational beings." But when he begins to deduce any of the actual duties of morality from this precept, he fails, almost grotesquely, to show that there would be any contradiction, any logical (not to say physical) impossibility, in all rational beings adopting the most outrageously immoral rules of conduct. All he shows is that the _consequences_ of their universal adoption would be such as no one would choose to incur.

On the present occasion, I shall set aside further discussion of the other theories. I shall try to contribute something toward the understanding and appreciation of the Utilitarian or Happiness theory, and toward such proof as it admits of. It is evident that this cannot be proof in the ordinary and popular meaning of the term. Direct proof is not available for questions of ultimate ends. To prove that anything is good, one must show it to be a means to something that is admitted to be good without proof. We prove the medical art good by showing that it leads to health, but how can anyone prove that health is good? The art of music is good, for the reason among others that it produces pleasure, but what proof is it possible to give that pleasure is good? If, then, it is asserted that there is a comprehensive formula that includes all things that are in themselves good, and that whatever else is good is so not as an end but as a means, the formula may be accepted or rejected, but it is not a subject of what is commonly understood by proof. We are not, however, to infer that accepting or rejecting it must depend on blind impulse or arbitrary choice. There is a larger meaning of the word proof, in which this question is as open to it as any other disputed question in philosophy. The subject is within the cognizance of the rational faculty, and that faculty does not handle it by intuition alone. Considerations can be presented that are capable of determining the intellect either to give or to withhold its assent to the doctrine, and this is equivalent to proof.

Presently we shall examine the nature of these considerations and how they bear on the case, and so what rational grounds can be given for accepting or rejecting the utilitarian formula. First, though, rational acceptance or rejection requires that the formula be correctly understood. I believe that the very imperfect notion ordinarily formed of its meaning is the chief obstacle to its reception. I believe also that if this notion could be cleared of even its grosser misconceptions, the question would be greatly simplified and a large proportion of its difficulties removed. Before I try to enter into the philosophical grounds that can be given for assenting to the utilitarian standard, therefore, I shall offer some illustrations of the doctrine itself. I want to show more clearly what it is and to distinguish it from what it is not. I also want to dispose of those practical objections that either arise from mistaken interpretations of its meaning or are closely tied to them. With the ground thus prepared, I shall afterward endeavor to throw such light as I can on the question, considered as one of philosophical theory.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 — What Utilitarianism Is
paragraphs: The idea that those who defend utility as the test of right and wrong use the word in its narrow, everyday sense, in which utility is the opposite of pleasure, is an ignorant blunder, and it needs only a passing remark. The philosophical opponents of utilitarianism are owed an apology, even for seeming for a moment to confuse them with anyone capable of so absurd a misconception. It is all the more extraordinary because another common charge against utilitarianism says the opposite: that it refers everything to pleasure, and to pleasure in its grossest form. As an able writer has pointedly remarked, the same sort of people, and often the very same people, denounce the theory "as impracticably dry when the word utility precedes the word pleasure, and as too practicably voluptuous when the word pleasure precedes the word utility." Those who know anything about the subject are aware that every writer who upheld the theory of utility, from Epicurus to Bentham, meant by it not something set against pleasure but pleasure itself, together with freedom from pain. Instead of opposing the useful to the agreeable or the ornamental, they have always declared that the useful includes these, among other things. Yet the common herd, including the herd of writers, keep falling into this shallow mistake, not only in newspapers and periodicals but in books of weight and pretension. They have picked up the word utilitarian while knowing nothing about it but its sound, and they habitually use it to mean the rejection, or neglect, of pleasure in some of its forms: of beauty, of ornament, or of amusement. The term is not misapplied in this ignorant way only to disparage; occasionally it is used as a compliment, as though it implied a superiority to frivolity and the mere pleasures of the moment. This perverted use is the only one in which the word is popularly known, and the new generation are getting their only notion of its meaning from it. Those who introduced the word, but had for many years given up using it as a distinctive name, may well feel called on to take it up again, if by doing so they can hope to do anything toward rescuing it from this utter degradation.[A]

The creed that takes utility, or the Greatest Happiness Principle, as the foundation of morals holds that actions are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness, and wrong in proportion as they tend to produce the reverse of happiness. Happiness here means pleasure and the absence of pain; unhappiness means pain and the lack of pleasure. To give a clear view of the moral standard this theory sets up, much more needs to be said. In particular, we must say what it includes in the ideas of pain and pleasure, and how far that is left an open question. But these supplementary explanations leave untouched the theory of life on which the theory of morality rests. That theory holds that pleasure and freedom from pain are the only things desirable as ends. It also holds that all desirable things (which are as numerous in the utilitarian scheme as in any other) are desirable either for the pleasure inherent in themselves or as means to promoting pleasure and preventing pain.

Now, such a theory of life arouses in many minds, including some of the most estimable in feeling and purpose, a deep-rooted dislike. To suppose that life has (as they put it) no higher end than pleasure, no better and nobler object of desire and pursuit, they designate as utterly mean and grovelling. They call it a doctrine worthy only of swine, to whom the followers of Epicurus were contemptuously likened at a very early period; and the modern holders of the doctrine are occasionally the subject of equally polite comparisons by their German, French, and English assailants.

The Epicureans have always replied to this attack by saying that the ones who degrade human nature are not they but their accusers, because the accusation takes human beings to be capable only of the pleasures that swine are capable of. If that were true, nobody could deny the charge, but it would then stop being an imputation at all. If human beings and swine drew pleasure from exactly the same sources, a rule of life good enough for one would be good enough for the other. Comparing the Epicurean life with a beast's life feels degrading for just this reason: a beast's pleasures do not meet a human being's conceptions of happiness. Human beings have faculties that rank above the animal appetites. Once they are aware of those faculties, they count nothing as happiness unless it also gratifies them. I do not, indeed, consider the Epicureans to have been by any means faultless in working out the consequences of the utilitarian principle. Doing that adequately would take in many Stoic as well as Christian elements. But no Epicurean theory of life that we know of fails to rate the pleasures of the intellect, of the feelings and imagination, and of the moral sentiments far above the pleasures of mere sensation. It must be admitted, however, that utilitarian writers in general have found the superiority of mental over bodily pleasures chiefly in the greater permanency, safety, uncostliness, &c., of the former — that is, in their circumstantial advantages rather than in their intrinsic nature. They have fully proved their case on all these points. But they could, with entire consistency, have taken the other ground, which may be called higher. The principle of utility is quite compatible with recognizing that some _kinds_ of pleasure are more desirable and more valuable than others. It would be absurd to say that quality counts alongside quantity when we estimate everything else, yet that pleasures are to be estimated by quantity alone.

Suppose I am asked what I mean by a difference of quality in pleasures, or what, apart from being greater in amount, makes one pleasure more valuable than another merely as a pleasure. There is only one possible answer. Of two pleasures, the more desirable is the one that all, or almost all, who have experienced both decidedly prefer, whether or not they feel any moral obligation to prefer it. Suppose those who are competently acquainted with both rank one so far above the other that they prefer it even knowing it brings a greater amount of discontent, and would not trade it for any quantity of the other pleasure their nature can enjoy. Then we are justified in saying that the preferred enjoyment is superior in quality, so far outweighing quantity that, by comparison, quantity hardly counts.

Now it is an unquestionable fact that people who know both kinds of pleasure equally well, and are equally able to appreciate and enjoy both, markedly prefer the way of life that engages their higher faculties. Few human creatures would accept being turned into one of the lower animals, even for a promise of the fullest share of a beast's pleasures. No intelligent person would agree to be a fool, no instructed person an ignoramus, no person of feeling and conscience selfish and base, even if convinced that the fool, the dunce, or the rascal is better satisfied with his lot than they are with theirs. They would not trade away what they have beyond what he has, not even for the complete satisfaction of every desire they share with him. If they ever imagine they would, it is only in a state of unhappiness so extreme that they would swap their lot for almost any other to escape it, however undesirable they found that other lot. A being with higher faculties needs more in order to be happy, is probably able to suffer more acutely, and is certainly exposed to suffering at more points than a being of an inferior type. Despite all this, he can never truly wish to sink into what he feels to be a lower grade of existence. We may explain this unwillingness however we like. We may put it down to pride, a name that gets applied without distinction to some of the most and some of the least estimable feelings mankind has. We may trace it to the love of liberty and personal independence, which the Stoics appealed to as one of the most effective ways of teaching it; or to the love of power, or to the love of excitement, both of which really do play a part in it. But the name that fits it best is a sense of dignity. Every human being has this in one form or another, and in some it matches their higher faculties, though by no means exactly. For those in whom it is strong, it is so essential a part of their happiness that nothing in conflict with it could attract them, except for a moment. Anyone who supposes that this preference costs the superior being some happiness — that he is not happier than the inferior one in anything like equal circumstances — is confounding two very different ideas, happiness and content. It is indisputable that a being with low capacities for enjoyment has the best chance of satisfying them fully, while a highly endowed being will always feel that whatever happiness he can look for, in the world as it is, is imperfect. But he can learn to put up with its imperfections, if they are at all bearable. And they will not make him envy the being who is unconscious of them, since that being is unconscious only because he does not feel at all the good which those imperfections qualify. It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied. And if the fool, or the pig, is of a different opinion, it is because they only know their own side of the question. The other party to the comparison knows both sides.

It may be objected that many people who are capable of the higher pleasures sometimes, under temptation, give the lower ones priority over them. But this fits perfectly well with fully appreciating how superior the higher pleasures are in themselves. Men often choose the nearer good out of weakness of character, though they know it is the less valuable. They do this just as much when choosing between two bodily pleasures as when choosing between a bodily and a mental one. They indulge their senses at the cost of their health, though they know perfectly well that health is the greater good. It may be objected further that many who start out with youthful enthusiasm for everything noble sink, as the years pass, into indolence and selfishness. But I do not believe that people who go through this very common change choose the lower pleasures over the higher ones of their own free will. I believe that, before they give themselves wholly to the one kind, they have already lost the capacity for the other. In most natures the capacity for the nobler feelings is a very tender plant. Hostile influences kill it easily, and so does simple lack of nourishment. In most young people it quickly withers if their occupations, fixed by their position in life, and the society they have been thrown into, do not help to keep that higher capacity in use. Men lose their high aspirations just as they lose their intellectual tastes: they have no time or opportunity to indulge them. And they take to inferior pleasures not through any deliberate preference, but because those are the only pleasures within their reach, or the only ones they can still enjoy. It may be questioned whether anyone who has stayed equally susceptible to both classes of pleasures has ever knowingly and calmly preferred the lower, though in every age many have broken down in a futile attempt to combine both.

From this verdict of the only competent judges, I understand there can be no appeal. Suppose the question is which of two pleasures is the more worth having, or which of two modes of existence is the more agreeable to the feelings, apart from its moral attributes and from its consequences. The judgment of those who are qualified by knowledge of both — or, if they differ, of the majority among them — must be accepted as final. We need hesitate the less to accept this judgment about the quality of pleasures, since there is no other tribunal to refer to even on the question of quantity. What means is there of determining which of two pains is the more acute, or which of two pleasurable sensations is the more intense, except the general vote of those familiar with both? Neither pains nor pleasures are homogeneous, and pain is always heterogeneous with pleasure. What is there to decide whether a particular pleasure is worth buying at the cost of a particular pain, except the feelings and judgment of the experienced? When, therefore, those feelings and that judgment declare the pleasures derived from the higher faculties to be preferable _in kind_, apart from the question of intensity, to those that the animal nature, cut off from the higher faculties, is capable of, they are entitled to the same regard on this subject.

I have dwelt on this point because a perfectly just conception of Utility or Happiness, as the rule that directs human conduct, requires it. But accepting the utilitarian standard does not by any means depend on it. The standard is not the agent's own greatest happiness; it is the greatest amount of happiness altogether. It may possibly be doubted whether a noble character is always happier for being noble. There can be no doubt, though, that it makes other people happier, and that the world at large gains immensely from it. So utilitarianism could reach its end only by cultivating nobleness of character generally, even if each person benefited only from other people's nobleness and his own, so far as happiness is concerned, were a sheer deduction from that benefit. But merely stating such an absurdity as this last makes refutation superfluous.

According to the Greatest Happiness Principle, as explained above, the ultimate end is an existence as free from pain as possible and as rich as possible in enjoyments, both in quantity and in quality. It is the end with reference to which, and for the sake of which, all other things are desirable (whether we are considering our own good or that of other people). The test of quality, and the rule for measuring it against quantity, is the preference felt by those who are best furnished with the means of comparison, through their opportunities of experience, to which must be added their habits of self-consciousness and self-observation. According to the utilitarian opinion, this is the end of human action, and so it is necessarily also the standard of morality. Morality may accordingly be defined as the rules and precepts for human conduct by the observance of which an existence such as has been described might be secured, to the greatest extent possible, to all mankind; and not to them only but, so far as the nature of things allows, to the whole sentient creation.

Against this doctrine, however, another class of objectors arises. They say that happiness, in any form, cannot be the rational purpose of human life and action. In the first place, they say, it cannot be attained; and they ask with contempt, What right hast thou to be happy? Mr. Carlyle drives the question home by adding, What right, a short time ago, hadst thou even _to be_? In the next place, they say that men can do _without_ happiness. All noble human beings, they say, have felt this, and could only have become noble by learning the lesson of Entsagen, or renunciation. They affirm that this lesson, once thoroughly learned and accepted, is the beginning and the necessary condition of all virtue.

If the first of these objections were well founded, it would go to the root of the matter. If human beings cannot have any happiness at all, then attaining it cannot be the end of morality or of any rational conduct. Even so, something could still be said for the utilitarian theory. Utility covers not just the pursuit of happiness but also preventing or lessening unhappiness. If the pursuit of happiness is a chimera, the need to prevent unhappiness becomes all the more urgent and has all the more room to work — at least so long as mankind think fit to go on living, and do not take refuge in the simultaneous suicide that Novalis recommended under certain conditions. Still, when someone flatly asserts that human life cannot be happy, the assertion is at least an exaggeration, if it is not something like a verbal quibble. If happiness means an unbroken run of highly pleasurable excitement, then it is evident enough that happiness is impossible. A state of exalted pleasure lasts only for moments, or in some cases, with some breaks, for hours or days. It is the occasional brilliant flash of enjoyment, not its permanent and steady flame. The philosophers who taught that happiness is the end of life knew this as well as those who taunt them. What they meant by happiness was not a life of rapture. They meant moments of rapture within an existence that has few and fleeting pains, many and varied pleasures, a decided predominance of the active over the passive, and, as the foundation of the whole, the principle of not expecting more from life than it can give. Those fortunate enough to have such a life have always thought it deserved the name of happiness. And such an existence is even now the lot of many, for a considerable part of their lives. Our present wretched education and wretched social arrangements are the only real hindrance to almost everyone's being able to have it.

The objectors may perhaps doubt that human beings, if taught to regard happiness as the end of life, would be satisfied with so moderate a share of it. But great numbers of people have been satisfied with much less. A satisfied life appears to consist mainly of two things, and often either one alone is enough: tranquillity and excitement. Many people with plenty of tranquillity find they can be content with very little pleasure; many with plenty of excitement can make their peace with a considerable amount of pain. There is surely no inherent impossibility in enabling even the mass of mankind to combine both. The two are far from incompatible; they are natural allies, since a long stretch of either prepares the way for the other and awakens a wish for it. Only people whose indolence has become a vice fail to want excitement after a period of rest. Only people for whom the need of excitement is a disease find the tranquillity that follows excitement dull and flat, when it ought to be pleasurable in direct proportion to the excitement before it. Suppose people who are tolerably fortunate in their outward circumstances do not find enough enjoyment in life to make it valuable to them. The cause, generally, is that they care for nobody but themselves. Those who have no public or private affections have far fewer of life's excitements, and in any case those excitements lose value as the time draws near when death must end all selfish interests. Those who leave behind people they love, and especially those who have also cultivated fellow-feeling with the collective interests of mankind, take as lively an interest in life on the eve of death as they did in the vigor of youth and health. After selfishness, the chief cause of an unsatisfactory life is lack of mental cultivation. A cultivated mind — I do not mean a philosopher's, but any mind to which the fountains of knowledge have been opened and which has been taught, to any tolerable degree, to use its faculties — finds inexhaustible interest in everything around it: in the objects of nature, the achievements of art, the imaginations of poetry, the incidents of history, the ways of mankind past and present, and their prospects for the future. It is possible, indeed, to grow indifferent to all of this, even without having exhausted a thousandth part of it. But that happens only to someone who from the start took no moral or human interest in these things and looked in them only to gratify curiosity.

Now there is absolutely no reason in the nature of things why everyone born in a civilized country should not inherit enough mental culture to take an intelligent interest in these objects of contemplation. There is just as little inherent necessity for any human being to be a selfish egotist, with no feeling or care except for what centers on his own miserable individuality. Something far better than that is common enough even now to give ample earnest of what the human species may be made. Every rightly brought-up human being can have genuine private affections and a sincere interest in the public good, though not in equal degrees. The world holds so much to interest, so much to enjoy, and so much also to correct and improve. In such a world, anyone with this moderate stock of moral and intellectual requisites can live an existence that may be called enviable. He will not fail to find this enviable existence, provided that bad laws or subjection to the will of others do not deny him the liberty to use the sources of happiness within his reach, and provided that he escapes the positive evils of life, the great sources of physical and mental suffering — such as indigence, disease, and the unkindness, worthlessness, or premature loss of those he loves. The main stress of the problem therefore lies in the struggle against these calamities. Escaping them entirely is a rare good fortune. As things now are, they cannot be avoided, and often cannot be lessened in any material degree. Yet no one whose opinion deserves a moment's consideration can doubt that most of the great positive evils of the world can be removed in themselves, and that, if human affairs continue to improve, they will in the end be reduced within narrow limits. The wisdom of society, joined with the good sense and providence of individuals, may completely extinguish poverty in any sense that involves suffering. Even disease, that most intractable of enemies, may be reduced without limit by good physical and moral education and proper control of noxious influences; and the progress of science promises still more direct conquests over this detestable foe in the future. Each advance in that direction frees us from some of the chances that cut short our own lives and, what concerns us still more, from those that take away the people our happiness is wrapped up in. As for vicissitudes of fortune and other disappointments connected with worldly circumstances, they come mainly from gross imprudence, from ill-regulated desires, or from bad or imperfect social institutions. In short, human care and effort can conquer all the grand sources of human suffering to a great degree, and many of them almost entirely. Removing them is grievously slow. A long succession of generations will perish in the breach before the conquest is completed and this world becomes all that it might easily be made if will and knowledge were not wanting. Yet any mind intelligent and generous enough to take a part in the endeavor, however small and unconspicuous, will draw a noble enjoyment from the struggle itself. He would not agree to give that up for any bribe of selfish indulgence.

This brings us to a true estimate of what the objectors say about the possibility, and the obligation, of learning to do without happiness. It is unquestionably possible to do without happiness. Nineteen-twentieths of mankind do it involuntarily, even in the parts of our present world that are least deep in barbarism. The hero or the martyr often has to do it voluntarily, for the sake of something he prizes more than his individual happiness. But what is this something, if it is not the happiness of others, or some of the requisites of happiness? It is noble to be able to give up entirely one's own share of happiness, or one's chances of it. But after all, the self-sacrifice must be made for some end; it is not its own end. We may be told that its end is not happiness but virtue, which is better than happiness. To that I ask: would the hero or martyr make the sacrifice if he did not believe it would spare others from having to make similar sacrifices? Would he make it if he thought his giving up happiness for himself would bear no fruit for any of his fellow creatures, except to make their lot like his and put them too among those who have renounced happiness? All honor to those who can give up for themselves the personal enjoyment of life, when by doing so they worthily add to the amount of happiness in the world. But a person who does it, or claims to do it, for any other purpose deserves no more admiration than the ascetic on his pillar. He may be an inspiriting proof of what men _can_ do, but assuredly not an example of what they _should_.

Anyone can best serve the happiness of others by the absolute sacrifice of his own only when the world's arrangements are in a very imperfect state. But so long as the world is in that imperfect state, I fully acknowledge that readiness to make such a sacrifice is the highest virtue to be found in man. I will add something that may sound paradoxical: in the world as it now is, the conscious ability to do without happiness offers the best prospect of attaining whatever happiness can be attained. Nothing but that consciousness can lift a person above the chances of life. It makes him feel that, whatever fate and fortune may do, they have no power to subdue him. Once he feels this, he is free of excessive anxiety about the evils of life. Like many a Stoic in the worst times of the Roman Empire, he can then calmly cultivate the sources of satisfaction open to him. He does not trouble himself about how long they will last, any more than about their inevitable end.

In the meantime, utilitarians should never stop claiming the morality of self-devotion as their own possession, to which they have as good a right as the Stoic or the Transcendentalist. Utilitarian morality does recognize that human beings have the power to sacrifice their own greatest good for the good of others. What it refuses to admit is that the sacrifice is itself a good. A sacrifice that does not increase the sum total of happiness, or tend to increase it, it regards as wasted. The only self-renunciation it applauds is devotion to the happiness of others, or to some of the means of happiness: whether the happiness of mankind collectively, or of individuals within the limits set by the collective interests of mankind.

I must repeat something that the assailants of utilitarianism seldom have the justice to acknowledge. The happiness that forms the utilitarian standard of what is right in conduct is not the agent's own happiness, but the happiness of all concerned. Between his own happiness and that of others, utilitarianism requires him to be as strictly impartial as a disinterested and benevolent spectator. In the golden rule of Jesus of Nazareth we read the complete spirit of the ethics of utility. To do as one would be done by, and to love one's neighbor as oneself, make up the ideal perfection of utilitarian morality. To come as near to this ideal as possible, utility would enjoin two things. First, laws and social arrangements should bring the happiness of every individual into the closest possible harmony with the interest of the whole. (Speaking practically, this happiness may be called his interest.) Second, education and opinion have a vast power over human character, and they should use that power to establish in every individual's mind an indissoluble association between his own happiness and the good of the whole. They should especially tie his own happiness to the practice of those modes of conduct, negative and positive, that regard for the universal happiness prescribes. The result would be that he could not even conceive happiness for himself that was consistent with conduct opposed to the general good. It would also be that a direct impulse to promote the general good would be, in every individual, one of the habitual motives of action, and the sentiments connected with it would fill a large and prominent place in every human being's sentient existence. Suppose the critics of utilitarian morality pictured it to themselves in this, its true character. I do not know what recommendation of any other morality they could possibly say it lacked. I do not know what more beautiful or more exalted developments of human nature they could suppose any other ethical system to foster. And I do not know what springs of action, closed to the utilitarian, such systems rely on to give effect to their commands.

We cannot always charge the objectors to utilitarianism with showing it in a discreditable light. On the contrary, those among them who have anything like a just idea of its disinterested character sometimes find fault with its standard for being too high for humanity. They say it demands too much to require that people always act from the inducement of promoting the general interests of society. But this mistakes the very meaning of a standard of morals, and confuses the rule of action with the motive for it. It is the business of ethics to tell us what our duties are, or by what test we may know them. No system of ethics requires that the sole motive of everything we do be a feeling of duty. On the contrary, ninety-nine hundredths of all our actions are done from other motives, and rightly so done, if the rule of duty does not condemn them. It is all the more unjust to utilitarianism that this misapprehension should be made a ground of objection to it, because utilitarian moralists have gone further than almost all others in affirming that the motive has nothing to do with the morality of the action, though it has much to do with the worth of the agent. He who saves a fellow creature from drowning does what is morally right, whether his motive is duty or the hope of being paid for his trouble. He who betrays a friend that trusts him is guilty of a crime, even if his aim is to serve another friend to whom he owes greater obligations.[B] But let us speak only of actions done from the motive of duty, in direct obedience to principle. Even here it is a misapprehension of the utilitarian way of thinking to suppose it implies that people should fix their minds on so wide a generality as the world, or society at large. The great majority of good actions are intended not for the benefit of the world but for that of individuals, and the good of the world is made up of these. On such occasions the thoughts of the most virtuous man need not travel beyond the particular persons concerned. The one exception is that he must make sure that in benefiting them he is not violating the rights of anyone else, that is, their legitimate and authorized expectations. According to the utilitarian ethics, the multiplication of happiness is the object of virtue. But the occasions on which any person (except one in a thousand) has it in his power to do this on an extended scale, in other words to be a public benefactor, are only exceptional. On those occasions alone is he called on to consider public utility. In every other case, private utility, the interest or happiness of some few persons, is all he has to attend to. Only those whose actions influence society in general need habitually concern themselves with so large an object. In the case of abstinences, it is different. These are things people refrain from doing for moral reasons, though the consequences in the particular case might be beneficial. Here it would be unworthy of an intelligent agent not to be consciously aware that the action belongs to a class which, if practiced generally, would be generally injurious, and that this is the ground of the obligation to abstain from it. The amount of regard for the public interest that this recognition implies is no greater than every system of morals demands, for they all enjoin abstaining from whatever is manifestly pernicious to society.

The same considerations dispose of another reproach against the doctrine of utility. This one rests on a still grosser misconception of the purpose of a standard of morality, and of the very meaning of the words right and wrong. It is often affirmed that utilitarianism makes men cold and unsympathizing. It is said to chill their moral feelings toward individuals, and to make them look only at the dry and hard question of the consequences of actions, without taking into their moral estimate the qualities from which those actions come. Suppose the assertion means that they do not let their judgment of the rightness or wrongness of an action be influenced by their opinion of the qualities of the person who does it. Then this is a complaint not against utilitarianism but against having any standard of morality at all. Certainly no known ethical standard decides that an action is good or bad because a good or a bad man does it, still less because an amiable, a brave or a benevolent man does it, or the contrary. These considerations bear not on the estimation of actions but on that of persons. And nothing in the utilitarian theory conflicts with the fact that other things besides the rightness and wrongness of their actions interest us in persons. The Stoics, indeed, misused language paradoxically, as part of their system, in their effort to rise above all concern with anything but virtue. They were fond of saying that he who has virtue has everything, and that he, and only he, is rich, is beautiful, is a king. But the utilitarian doctrine makes no claim of this kind for the virtuous man. Utilitarians are quite aware that there are other desirable possessions and qualities besides virtue, and they are perfectly willing to allow all of them their full worth. They are also aware that a right action does not necessarily show a virtuous character, and that blameable actions often come from qualities that deserve praise. When this is evident in a particular case, it changes their estimation, not certainly of the act, but of the agent. I grant that they nevertheless hold that in the long run the best proof of a good character is good actions. They also resolutely refuse to consider any mental disposition good if its predominant tendency is to produce bad conduct. This makes them unpopular with many people. But it is an unpopularity they must share with everyone who takes the distinction between right and wrong seriously, and a conscientious utilitarian need not be anxious to repel the reproach.

Suppose the objection means no more than this: many utilitarians look at the morality of actions, as measured by the utilitarian standard, with too exclusive a regard, and do not lay enough stress on the other beauties of character that make a human being lovable or admirable. This may be admitted. Utilitarians who have cultivated their moral feelings but not their sympathies or their artistic perceptions do fall into this mistake, and so do all other moralists in the same condition. What can be said in excuse for other moralists is equally available for them: if there is to be any error, it is better that it be on that side. As a matter of fact, we may affirm that among utilitarians, as among adherents of other systems, there is every imaginable degree of rigidity and of laxity in applying their standard. Some are even puritanically rigorous, while others are as indulgent as any sinner or sentimentalist could wish. But on the whole, a doctrine that puts so prominently forward the interest mankind has in repressing and preventing conduct that violates the moral law is likely to be inferior to no other in turning the sanctions of opinion against such violations. It is true that the question "What does violate the moral law?" is one on which those who recognize different standards of morality are likely now and then to differ. But utilitarianism did not first introduce disagreement on moral questions into the world. And that doctrine does supply a tangible and intelligible way of deciding such disagreements, if not always an easy one.

It may not be superfluous to notice a few more of the common misapprehensions of utilitarian ethics. Some are so obvious and gross that it might seem impossible for any person of candor and intelligence to fall into them. Yet persons of considerable mental endowments often take so little trouble to understand the bearings of an opinion they are prejudiced against. And men are in general so little conscious of this voluntary ignorance as a defect that the vulgarest misunderstandings of ethical doctrines are continually found in the deliberate writings of people with the greatest pretensions to high principle and to philosophy. We not uncommonly hear the doctrine of utility denounced as a _godless_ doctrine. If anything need be said against so mere an assumption, we may say that the question depends on the idea we have formed of the moral character of the Deity. Suppose it is a true belief that God desires, above all things, the happiness of his creatures, and that this was his purpose in creating them. Then utility is not only not a godless doctrine, it is more profoundly religious than any other. Suppose it is meant instead that utilitarianism does not recognize the revealed will of God as the supreme law of morals. I answer that a utilitarian who believes in the perfect goodness and wisdom of God necessarily believes that whatever God has thought fit to reveal on the subject of morals must fulfill the requirements of utility in a supreme degree. But others besides utilitarians have held that the Christian revelation was intended, and is fitted, to fill the hearts and minds of mankind with a spirit that would enable them to find for themselves what is right, and incline them to do it when found. On this view it was not meant to tell them what it is, except in a very general way. They also hold that we need a carefully developed doctrine of ethics to _interpret_ to us the will of God. Whether this opinion is correct or not, it is superfluous to discuss here. Whatever aid religion, natural or revealed, can give to ethical investigation is as open to the utilitarian moralist as to any other. He can use it as the testimony of God to the usefulness or hurtfulness of any given course of action, with as good a right as others have to use it to indicate a transcendental law that has no connection with usefulness or with happiness.

Again, Utility is often stigmatized summarily as an immoral doctrine, by giving it the name of Expediency and exploiting the popular use of that term to contrast it with Principle. But the Expedient, in the sense in which it is opposed to the Right, generally means what is expedient for the particular interest of the agent himself, as when a minister sacrifices the interest of his country to keep himself in office. When it means anything better than this, it means what is expedient for some immediate object or temporary purpose, but violates a rule whose observance is expedient in a much higher degree. The Expedient in this sense, far from being the same thing as the useful, is a branch of the hurtful. Thus it would often be expedient to tell a lie, in order to get over some momentary embarrassment, or to gain some object immediately useful to ourselves or others. But there are two points to weigh. First, cultivating in ourselves a sensitive feeling about veracity is one of the most useful things our conduct can serve, and weakening that feeling is one of the most hurtful. Second, any deviation from truth, even an unintentional one, does that much to weaken the trustworthiness of human assertion. That trustworthiness is the principal support of all present social well-being, and its insufficiency does more than anything else that can be named to hold back civilization, virtue, and everything on which human happiness on the largest scale depends. So we feel that violating a rule of such transcendent expediency, for the sake of a present advantage, is not expedient. And we feel that whoever, for the sake of a convenience to himself or to some other individual, does what he can to deprive mankind of the good involved in being able to rely on each other's word, and to inflict on them the corresponding evil, acts the part of one of their worst enemies. Yet all moralists acknowledge that even this rule, sacred as it is, admits of possible exceptions. The chief exception is this: the withholding of some fact (such as information from a malefactor, or bad news from a person dangerously ill) would save someone from great and unmerited evil (especially someone other than oneself), and the withholding can be done only by denial. But the exception should not extend itself beyond the need, and should have the least possible effect in weakening reliance on veracity. So it ought to be recognized and, if possible, its limits defined. And if the principle of utility is good for anything, it must be good for weighing these conflicting utilities against one another, and marking out the region within which one or the other preponderates.

Again, defenders of utility often find themselves called on to answer objections like this one: there is not time, before acting, to calculate and weigh the effects of any line of conduct on the general happiness. This is exactly as if someone were to say that it is impossible to guide our conduct by Christianity, because on every occasion when something has to be done there is not time to read through the Old and New Testaments. The answer to the objection is that there has been ample time, namely the whole past duration of the human species. During all that time mankind have been learning by experience the tendencies of actions, and all the prudence of life, as well as all its morality, depends on that experience. People talk as if the beginning of this course of experience had until now been put off. They talk as if, at the moment a man feels tempted to meddle with the property or life of another, he had to begin considering for the first time whether murder and theft are injurious to human happiness. Even then I do not think he would find the question very puzzling. At all events, the matter has now been done for him. It is truly a whimsical supposition that if mankind agreed in considering utility to be the test of morality, they would remain without any agreement as to what is useful, and would take no measures to have their notions on the subject taught to the young and enforced by law and opinion. It is easy to prove that any ethical standard whatever works ill, if we suppose universal idiocy to go along with it. But on any hypothesis short of that, mankind must by this time have acquired positive beliefs about the effects of some actions on their happiness. The beliefs that have thus come down are the rules of morality for the multitude, and for the philosopher until he succeeds in finding better ones. I admit, or rather earnestly maintain, three things: that philosophers might easily do this, even now, on many subjects; that the received code of ethics is by no means of divine right; and that mankind still have much to learn about the effects of actions on the general happiness. The corollaries from the principle of utility, like the precepts of every practical art, admit of indefinite improvement, and in a progressive state of the human mind that improvement is going on perpetually. But it is one thing to consider the rules of morality improvable. It is another thing to pass over the intermediate generalizations entirely and try to test each individual action directly by the first principle. It is a strange notion that acknowledging a first principle is inconsistent with admitting secondary ones. To tell a traveler the place of his ultimate destination is not to forbid the use of landmarks and direction-posts along the way. The proposition that happiness is the end and aim of morality does not mean that no road ought to be laid down to that goal, or that persons going there should not be advised to take one direction rather than another. Men really ought to stop talking a kind of nonsense on this subject that they would neither talk nor listen to on other matters of practical concern. Nobody argues that the art of navigation is not founded on astronomy because sailors cannot wait to calculate the Nautical Almanack. Being rational creatures, they go to sea with it already calculated. And all rational creatures go out upon the sea of life with their minds made up on the common questions of right and wrong, as well as on many of the far more difficult questions of wise and foolish. As long as foresight is a human quality, we may presume they will continue to do this. Whatever we adopt as the fundamental principle of morality, we need subordinate principles to apply it by. The impossibility of doing without them is common to all systems, so it can afford no argument against any one in particular. But to argue gravely as if no such secondary principles could be had, and as if mankind had until now remained, and always must remain, without drawing any general conclusions from the experience of human life, is as high a pitch, I think, as absurdity has ever reached in philosophical controversy.

Most of the remaining stock arguments against utilitarianism consist in blaming it for the common infirmities of human nature, and for the general difficulties that embarrass conscientious persons in shaping their course through life. We are told that a utilitarian will be apt to make his own particular case an exception to moral rules, and that, when under temptation, he will see more utility in breaking a rule than in keeping it. But is utility the only creed that can furnish us with excuses for evil doing, and with means of cheating our own conscience? All doctrines provide these in abundance if they recognize, as a fact in morals, the existence of conflicting considerations, and every doctrine believed by sane persons does. It is not the fault of any creed, but of the complicated nature of human affairs, that rules of conduct cannot be framed so as to require no exceptions, and that hardly any kind of action can safely be laid down as either always obligatory or always condemnable. No ethical creed fails to soften the rigidity of its laws by giving a certain latitude, under the moral responsibility of the agent, to accommodate peculiarities of circumstances. And under every creed, self-deception and dishonest casuistry get in at the opening thus made. There is no moral system under which unequivocal cases of conflicting obligation do not arise. These are the real difficulties, the knotty points both in the theory of ethics and in the conscientious guidance of personal conduct. People overcome them in practice with greater or less success according to their intellect and virtue. But it can hardly be pretended that anyone will be less qualified to deal with them for possessing an ultimate standard to which conflicting rights and duties can be referred. If utility is the ultimate source of moral obligations, utility may be invoked to decide between them when their demands are incompatible. Applying the standard may be difficult, but it is better than none at all. In other systems, the moral laws all claim independent authority, and there is no common umpire entitled to step in between them. Their claims to precedence over one another rest on little better than sophistry. Unless they are settled, as they generally are, by the unacknowledged influence of considerations of utility, they leave free scope for the action of personal desires and partialities. We must remember that only in these cases of conflict between secondary principles is it necessary to appeal to first principles. There is no case of moral obligation in which some secondary principle is not involved. And if only one is involved, there can seldom be any real doubt which one it is, in the mind of anyone who recognizes the principle itself.

[Footnote A: The author of this essay has reason to believe he was the first person to bring the word utilitarian into use. He did not invent it, but adopted it from a passing expression in Mr. Galt's _Annals of the Parish_. He used it as a designation for several years, and then he and others abandoned it, from a growing dislike of anything resembling a badge or watchword of sectarian distinction. But as a name for one single opinion, not a set of opinions, to denote the recognition of utility as a standard and not any particular way of applying it, the term fills a want in the language. In many cases it offers a convenient way of avoiding tiresome circumlocution.]

[Footnote B: An opponent, whose intellectual and moral fairness it is a pleasure to acknowledge (the Rev. J. Llewellyn Davis), has objected to this passage. He says, "Surely the rightness or wrongness of saving a man from drowning does depend very much upon the motive with which it is done. Suppose that a tyrant, when his enemy jumped into the sea to escape from him, saved him from drowning simply in order that he might inflict upon him more exquisite tortures, would it tend to clearness to speak of that rescue as 'a morally right action?' Or suppose again, according to one of the stock illustrations of ethical inquiries, that a man betrayed a trust received from a friend, because the discharge of it would fatally injure that friend himself or some one belonging to him, would utilitarianism compel one to call the betrayal 'a crime' as much as if it had been done from the meanest motive?" I submit that the man who saves another from drowning in order to kill him by torture afterward does not differ from the man who does the same thing from duty or benevolence in motive only. The act itself is different. In the case supposed, the rescue is only the necessary first step of an act far more atrocious than leaving him to drown would have been. Suppose Mr. Davis had said, "The rightness or wrongness of saving a man from drowning does depend very much" — not upon the motive, but — "upon the _intention_." No utilitarian would have differed from him. Through an oversight too common not to be quite venial, Mr. Davis has in this case confounded the very different ideas of Motive and Intention. There is no point that utilitarian thinkers (and Bentham pre-eminently) have taken more pains to illustrate. The morality of the action depends entirely on the intention, that is, on what the agent _wills to do_. But the motive, that is, the feeling that makes him will so to do, makes no difference in the morality when it makes none in the act. It does make a great difference in our moral estimation of the agent, especially if it indicates a good or a bad habitual _disposition_, a bent of character from which useful actions, or hurtful ones, are likely to arise.]

chapters.title: Chapter 3 — Of the Ultimate Sanction of the Principle of Utility
paragraphs: People often ask, and rightly, what the sanction of any proposed moral standard is. What are the motives to obey it? Or, more specifically, what is the source of its obligation? Where does it get its binding force? Moral philosophy must answer this question. It often takes the form of an objection to utilitarian morality, as if it applied to that morality more than to others, but it really arises for every standard. In fact, it arises whenever a person is called on to adopt a standard, or to rest morality on a basis he is not used to. For the customary morality, the one that education and opinion have made sacred, is the only one that presents itself to the mind with the feeling of being obligatory _in itself_. When a person is asked to believe that this morality _derives_ its obligation from some general principle that custom has not surrounded with the same halo, the claim strikes him as a paradox. The supposed corollaries seem to have more binding force than the original theorem, and the superstructure seems to stand better without what is presented as its foundation than with it. He says to himself, I feel that I am bound not to rob or murder, betray or deceive; but why am I bound to promote the general happiness? If my own happiness lies in something else, why may I not give that the preference?

If the utilitarian philosophy is right about the nature of the moral sense, this difficulty will always arise. It will go on arising until the influences that form moral character have taken the same hold of the principle that they have taken of some of its consequences. That will happen when, through better education, the feeling of unity with our fellow creatures is as deeply rooted in our character as the horror of crime is in an ordinarily well-brought-up young person, and as completely a part of our nature to our own consciousness. It cannot be doubted that Christ intended it to be so. In the meantime, however, the difficulty is not peculiar to the doctrine of utility. It is inherent in every attempt to analyze morality and reduce it to principles. Unless the principle is already invested in men's minds with as much sacredness as any of its applications, such an attempt always seems to strip those applications of part of their sanctity.

The principle of utility has all the sanctions that belong to any other system of morals, or at least there is no reason why it might not have them. Those sanctions are either external or internal. I need not speak at any length of the external sanctions. They are the hope of favor and the fear of displeasure from our fellow creatures or from the Ruler of the Universe. Along with these go whatever sympathy or affection we may have for our fellow creatures, or love and awe of Him, which incline us to do His will independently of selfish consequences. There is plainly no reason why all these motives for observance should not attach themselves to the utilitarian morality as completely and as powerfully as to any other. Indeed, those that concern our fellow creatures are sure to do so in proportion to the amount of general intelligence. For whether or not there is any other ground of moral obligation than the general happiness, men do desire happiness. However imperfect their own practice may be, they desire and commend all conduct in others toward themselves by which they think their happiness is promoted. As for the religious motive, if men believe in the goodness of God, as most profess to do, then those who think that conduciveness to the general happiness is the essence of good, or even only its criterion, must necessarily believe that it is also what God approves. So the whole force of external reward and punishment, whether physical or moral, and whether it comes from God or from our fellow men, becomes available to enforce the utilitarian morality, in proportion as that morality is recognized. The same holds for all the disinterested devotion to either that human nature admits of. And the more education and general cultivation are bent to this purpose, the more powerful that force becomes.

That is all I need say of external sanctions. The internal sanction of duty is one and the same, whatever our standard of duty may be. It is a feeling in our own mind: a pain, more or less intense, that goes with the violation of duty. In properly cultivated moral natures, in the more serious cases, it rises into a shrinking from the violation as an impossibility. When this feeling is disinterested, and connects itself with the pure idea of duty rather than with some particular form of it or with any merely accessory circumstances, it is the essence of Conscience. But in the complex phenomenon as it actually exists, the simple fact is in general encrusted all over with collateral associations. These come from sympathy, from love, and still more from fear; from all the forms of religious feeling; from the recollections of childhood and of all our past life; from self-esteem, from the desire for the esteem of others, and occasionally even from self-abasement. I understand this extreme complication to be the origin of the mystical character that tends to be attributed to the idea of moral obligation. The human mind has a tendency, of which there are many other examples, that leads it to this. It leads people to believe that the idea cannot possibly attach itself to any objects other than those which, by some supposed mysterious law, we find in our present experience to excite it. The binding force of the idea, however, consists in the existence of a mass of feeling that must be broken through in order to do what violates our standard of right. If we do violate that standard nevertheless, we shall probably have to face this feeling afterward in the form of remorse. Whatever theory we hold of the nature or origin of conscience, this is what essentially constitutes it.

The ultimate sanction of all morality (external motives apart) is therefore a subjective feeling in our own minds. So I see nothing embarrassing to those whose standard is utility in the question, what is the sanction of that particular standard? We may answer that it is the same as for all other moral standards: the conscientious feelings of mankind. Undoubtedly this sanction has no binding efficacy on those who do not have the feelings it appeals to. But these persons will be no more obedient to any other moral principle than to the utilitarian one. On them morality of any kind has no hold except through the external sanctions. Meanwhile the feelings exist. They are a fact in human nature, and experience proves both their reality and the great power with which they can act on those in whom they have been duly cultivated. No reason has ever been shown why they may not be cultivated to as great an intensity in connection with the utilitarian rule as with any other rule of morals.

I am aware that there is a disposition to believe that a person who sees moral obligation as a transcendental fact, an objective reality belonging to the province of "Things in themselves," is likely to be more obedient to it than one who believes it to be entirely subjective, with its seat in human consciousness only. But whatever a person's opinion may be on this point of Ontology, the force that really urges him is his own subjective feeling, and it is exactly measured by that feeling's strength. No one's belief that Duty is an objective reality is stronger than the belief that God is one. Yet the belief in God, apart from the expectation of actual reward and punishment, affects conduct only through the subjective religious feeling, and only in proportion to it. So far as the sanction is disinterested, it is always in the mind itself. The notion of the transcendental moralists must therefore be this: that the sanction will not exist _in_ the mind unless it is believed to have its root outside the mind. And if a person can say to himself, That which is restraining me, and which is called my conscience, is only a feeling in my own mind, he may possibly conclude that when the feeling ceases the obligation ceases. He may conclude that if he finds the feeling inconvenient, he may disregard it and try to get rid of it. But is this danger confined to the utilitarian morality? Does the belief that moral obligation has its seat outside the mind make the feeling of it too strong to be got rid of? The fact is so far otherwise that all moralists admit and lament how easily, in the generality of minds, conscience can be silenced or stifled. The question, Need I obey my conscience? is put to themselves quite as often by persons who never heard of the principle of utility as by its adherents. Those whose conscientious feelings are so weak that they can ask this question will not answer it affirmatively, if they do, because they believe in the transcendental theory. They will do so because of the external sanctions.

For the present purpose, we need not decide whether the feeling of duty is innate or implanted. Suppose it is innate. Then it is an open question to what objects it naturally attaches itself, for the philosophic supporters of that theory now agree that what we perceive intuitively are principles of morality, not the details. If anything in the matter is innate, I see no reason why the innate feeling should not be that of regard to the pleasures and pains of others. If any principle of morals is intuitively obligatory, I should say it must be that one. If so, the intuitive ethics would coincide with the utilitarian, and there would be no further quarrel between them. Even as things stand, the intuitive moralists believe that there are other intuitive moral obligations, but they already believe this to be one of them. For they unanimously hold that a large part of morality turns on the consideration due to the interests of our fellow creatures. Therefore, if the belief in a transcendental origin of moral obligation gives any additional efficacy to the internal sanction, it appears to me that the utilitarian principle already has the benefit of it.

On the other hand, I believe the moral feelings are not innate but acquired. If so, they are not for that reason any less natural. It is natural to man to speak, to reason, to build cities, to cultivate the ground, though these are acquired faculties. The moral feelings are not indeed a part of our nature in the sense of being present, in any perceptible degree, in all of us. But this, unhappily, is a fact admitted even by those who most strenuously believe in their transcendental origin. The moral faculty is like the other acquired capacities I have mentioned. If it is not a part of our nature, it is a natural outgrowth from it. Like them, it can spring up spontaneously in a certain small degree, and cultivation can bring it to a high degree of development. Unhappily it can also, by sufficient use of the external sanctions and of the force of early impressions, be cultivated in almost any direction. So there is hardly anything so absurd or so mischievous that these influences cannot make it act on the human mind with all the authority of conscience. To doubt that the same means could give the same potency to the principle of utility, even if it had no foundation in human nature, would be flying in the face of all experience.

But moral associations that are wholly of artificial creation give way by degrees, as intellectual culture advances, to the dissolving force of analysis. Suppose the feeling of duty, when associated with utility, would appear equally arbitrary. Suppose there were no leading department of our nature, no powerful class of sentiments, with which that association would harmonize, which would make us feel it congenial, and which would incline us not only to foster it in others (for which we have abundant interested motives) but also to cherish it in ourselves. In short, suppose there were no natural basis of sentiment for utilitarian morality. Then it might well happen that this association too, even after education had implanted it, might be analyzed away.

But there is this basis of powerful natural sentiment. Once the general happiness is recognized as the ethical standard, this basis will constitute the strength of the utilitarian morality. This firm foundation is the social feelings of mankind: the desire to be in unity with our fellow creatures. It is already a powerful principle in human nature, and happily it is one of those that tend to grow stronger, even without express teaching, through the influences of advancing civilization. The social state is at once so natural, so necessary and so habitual to man that he never conceives himself otherwise than as a member of a body, except in some unusual circumstances or by an effort of voluntary abstraction. And this association is riveted more and more as mankind move further from the state of savage independence. Any condition that is essential to a state of society therefore becomes more and more an inseparable part of everyone's conception of the state of things into which he is born, which is the destiny of a human being. Now, society between human beings, except in the relation of master and slave, is manifestly impossible on any other footing than that the interests of all are to be consulted. Society between equals can exist only on the understanding that the interests of all are to be regarded equally. And in all states of civilization every person, except an absolute monarch, has equals. So everyone is obliged to live on these terms with somebody; and in every age some advance is made toward a state in which it will be impossible to live permanently on other terms with anybody. In this way people grow up unable to conceive as possible for them a state of total disregard of other people's interests. They are under a necessity of conceiving themselves as at least abstaining from all the grosser injuries, and (if only for their own protection) living in a state of constant protest against them. They are also familiar with co-operating with others and proposing to themselves a collective interest, not an individual one, as the aim (at least for the time being) of their actions. So long as they are co-operating, their ends are identified with those of others. There is at least a temporary feeling that the interests of others are their own interests. All strengthening of social ties, and all healthy growth of society, not only gives each individual a stronger personal interest in practically consulting the welfare of others. It also leads him to identify his feelings more and more with their good, or at least with an ever greater degree of practical consideration for it. He comes, as though instinctively, to be conscious of himself as a being who _of course_ pays regard to others. The good of others becomes to him something to be attended to naturally and necessarily, like any of the physical conditions of our existence. Now, whatever amount of this feeling a person has, the strongest motives of both interest and sympathy urge him to show it and to encourage it in others to the utmost of his power. Even if he has none of it himself, he has as great an interest as anyone else that others should have it. Consequently, the smallest germs of the feeling are seized on and nourished by the contagion of sympathy and the influences of education, and the powerful agency of the external sanctions weaves a complete web of corroborative association around it. As civilization goes on, this way of conceiving ourselves and human life is felt to be more and more natural. Every step in political improvement makes it more so. Each step removes sources of opposition of interest, and levels those inequalities of legal privilege between individuals or classes because of which there are still large portions of mankind whose happiness it is practicable to disregard. In an improving state of the human mind, the influences that tend to generate in each individual a feeling of unity with all the rest are constantly on the increase. If that feeling were perfect, he would never think of, or desire, any beneficial condition for himself in whose benefits they were not included. Now suppose this feeling of unity were taught as a religion. Suppose the whole force of education, of institutions and of opinion were directed to this end, as it once was in the case of religion, so that every person grew up from infancy surrounded on all sides by both the profession and the practice of it. I think that no one who can realize this conception will feel any misgiving about the sufficiency of the ultimate sanction for the Happiness morality. To any ethical student who finds the realization difficult, I recommend, as a means of making it easier, the second of M. Comte's two principal works, the _Système de Politique Positive_. I have the strongest objections to the system of politics and morals set out in that treatise. But I think it has more than amply shown that it is possible to give the service of humanity, even without the aid of belief in a Providence, both the physical power and the social efficacy of a religion. It can make that service take hold of human life and color all thought, feeling and action, in a manner of which the greatest ascendancy ever exercised by any religion may be only a type and foretaste. And the danger of it is not that it should be insufficient but that it should be so excessive as to interfere unduly with human freedom and individuality.

Nor do those who recognize the utilitarian morality need to wait for the social influences that would make its obligation felt by mankind at large, in order to have the feeling that constitutes its binding force. We live in a comparatively early state of human advancement. In it a person cannot indeed feel that entireness of sympathy with all others which would make any real discordance in the general direction of their conduct in life impossible. But already a person in whom the social feeling is at all developed cannot bring himself to think of the rest of his fellow creatures as struggling rivals for the means of happiness, whom he must desire to see defeated in their object so that he may succeed in his. Every individual even now has a deeply-rooted conception of himself as a social being.
