This tends to make him feel it one of his natural wants that there should be harmony between his feelings and aims and those of his fellow creatures. Differences of opinion and of mental culture may make it impossible for him to share many of their actual feelings, and perhaps make him denounce and defy those feelings. Even so, he still needs to be conscious that his real aim and theirs do not conflict. He needs to know that he is not opposing himself to what they really wish for, namely their own good, but is on the contrary promoting it. In most individuals this feeling is much inferior in strength to their selfish feelings, and it is often wanting altogether. But to those who have it, it has all the characters of a natural feeling. It does not present itself to their minds as a superstition of education, or a law despotically imposed by the power of society. It presents itself as an attribute that it would not be well for them to be without. This conviction is the ultimate sanction of the greatest-happiness morality. It is what makes any mind of well-developed feelings work with, and not against, the outward motives to care for others that are afforded by what I have called the external sanctions. And when those sanctions are wanting, or act in an opposite direction, this conviction in itself constitutes a powerful internal binding force, in proportion to the sensitiveness and thoughtfulness of the character. For few but those whose mind is a moral blank could bear to plan their course of life on the basis of paying no regard to others except so far as their own private interest compels.

chapters.title: Chapter 4 — Of What Sort of Proof the Principle of Utility Is Susceptible
paragraphs: It has already been remarked that questions of ultimate ends do not admit of proof, in the ordinary sense of the term. Every first principle is incapable of proof by reasoning. That is true of the first premises of our knowledge as well as of those of our conduct. But the first premises of knowledge are matters of fact. They may therefore be the subject of a direct appeal to the faculties that judge of fact, namely our senses and our internal consciousness. Can an appeal be made to the same faculties on questions of practical ends? Or by what other faculty do we take cognizance of them?

Questions about ends are, in other words, questions about what things are desirable. The utilitarian doctrine is that happiness is desirable, and is the only thing desirable, as an end; all other things are desirable only as means to that end. What should be required of this doctrine? What conditions must it fulfill to make good its claim to be believed?

Consider what proof there can be that an object is visible. The only proof is that people actually see it. Likewise the only proof that a sound is audible is that people hear it, and so with every other source of our experience. In the same way, I understand, the one piece of evidence we can offer that anything is desirable is that people do actually desire it. Suppose that, in theory and in practice, nobody acknowledged the end the utilitarian doctrine proposes to be an end. Then nothing could ever convince anyone that it was one. The only reason that can be given for the desirability of the general happiness is that each person, so far as he believes it attainable, desires his own happiness. Yet that is a fact. So we have not merely all the proof the case admits of, but all it is possible to ask for, that happiness is a good. Each person's happiness is a good to that person, and the general happiness is therefore a good to the aggregate of all persons. Happiness has made good its title as _one_ of the ends of conduct, and so as one of the criteria of morality.

But this alone has not proved it to be the sole criterion. By the same rule, it would seem necessary to show not only that people desire happiness but that they never desire anything else. Now it is plain that they do desire things that common language clearly distinguishes from happiness. For example, they desire virtue and the absence of vice, no less really than pleasure and the absence of pain. The desire of virtue is not as universal as the desire of happiness, but it is as authentic a fact. Hence the opponents of the utilitarian standard think they have a right to infer that there are other ends of human action besides happiness, and that happiness is not the standard of approbation and disapprobation.

But does the utilitarian doctrine deny that people desire virtue? Does it maintain that virtue is not a thing to be desired? The very reverse. It maintains that virtue is to be desired, and desired disinterestedly, for itself. Utilitarian moralists may hold any opinion about the original conditions that make virtue what it is. They may believe (as they do) that actions and dispositions are virtuous only because they promote some end other than virtue. Yet once this is granted, and once such considerations have settled what _is_ virtuous, they do two things. First, they put virtue at the very head of the things that are good as means to the ultimate end. Second, they recognize as a psychological fact that virtue may be, for the individual, a good in itself, with no looking to any end beyond it. They hold that the mind is not in a right state, not in a state conformable to Utility, not in the state most conducive to the general happiness, unless it loves virtue in this manner, as a thing desirable in itself. This holds even if, in the individual instance, virtue does not produce the other desirable consequences it tends to produce, and on account of which it is held to be virtue. This opinion is not in the smallest degree a departure from the Happiness principle. Happiness has very various ingredients, and each of them is desirable in itself, not merely when counted as swelling an aggregate. The principle of utility does not mean that a given pleasure, such as music, or a given exemption from pain, such as health, should be looked on as a means to some collective something called happiness, and desired on that account. They are desired and desirable in and for themselves. Besides being means, they are a part of the end. On the utilitarian doctrine, virtue is not naturally and originally part of the end, but it is capable of becoming so. In those who love it disinterestedly it has become so. They desire and cherish it not as a means to happiness but as a part of their happiness.

To illustrate this further, we may remember that virtue is not the only thing that was originally a means and would be and remain indifferent if it were not a means to anything else, but that comes, by association with what it is a means to, to be desired for itself, and with the utmost intensity. What, for example, shall we say of the love of money? There is nothing originally more desirable about money than about any heap of glittering pebbles. Its worth is solely that of the things it will buy, that is, the desires for other things than itself that it is a means of gratifying. Yet the love of money is not only one of the strongest moving forces of human life. In many cases money is desired in and for itself. The desire to possess it is often stronger than the desire to use it, and it goes on increasing when all the desires that point to ends beyond it, to be reached by means of it, are falling off. It may then be said truly that money is desired not for the sake of an end but as part of the end. From being a means to happiness, it has come to be itself a principal ingredient of the individual's conception of happiness. The same may be said of the majority of the great objects of human life, power for example, or fame. The one difference is that to each of these a certain amount of immediate pleasure is attached, which has at least the semblance of being naturally inherent in them; and that cannot be said of money. Still, the strongest natural attraction of both power and fame is the immense aid they give to the attainment of our other wishes. The strong association thus generated between them and all our objects of desire gives the direct desire of them the intensity it often assumes, so that in some characters it surpasses in strength all other desires. In these cases the means have become a part of the end, and a more important part of it than any of the things they are means to. What was once desired as an instrument for the attainment of happiness has come to be desired for its own sake. In being desired for its own sake, however, it is desired as part of happiness. The person is made happy, or thinks he would be made happy, by merely possessing it, and is made unhappy by failing to obtain it. The desire of it is not a different thing from the desire of happiness, any more than the love of music or the desire of health is. They are included in happiness. They are some of the elements of which the desire of happiness is made up. Happiness is not an abstract idea but a concrete whole, and these are some of its parts. And the utilitarian standard sanctions and approves their being so. Life would be a poor thing, very ill provided with sources of happiness, if nature did not make this provision. By it, things originally indifferent, but conducive to or otherwise associated with the satisfaction of our primitive desires, become in themselves sources of pleasure more valuable than the primitive pleasures, both in permanency, in the space of human existence they can cover, and even in intensity. According to the utilitarian conception, virtue is a good of this description. There was no original desire of it, or motive to it, except its conduciveness to pleasure, and especially to protection from pain. But through the association thus formed, it may be felt as a good in itself, and desired as such with as great an intensity as any other good. It differs from the love of money, of power or of fame in this way: all of these may, and often do, make the individual harmful to the other members of the society to which he belongs, whereas nothing makes him so much a blessing to them as the cultivation of the disinterested love of virtue. Consequently the utilitarian standard tolerates and approves those other acquired desires up to the point beyond which they would be more injurious to the general happiness than promotive of it. But it enjoins and requires the cultivation of the love of virtue up to the greatest strength possible, as being above all things important to the general happiness.

From the preceding considerations it follows that nothing is in reality desired except happiness. Anything desired otherwise than as a means to some end beyond itself, and ultimately to happiness, is desired as itself a part of happiness. It is not desired for itself until it has become so. Those who desire virtue for its own sake do so because being conscious of it is a pleasure, or because being conscious of lacking it is a pain, or for both reasons together. In truth pleasure and pain seldom come apart. Almost always they occur together, the same person feeling pleasure at the degree of virtue he has reached and pain at not having reached more. If the first gave him no pleasure and the second no pain, he would not love or desire virtue. Or he would desire it only for the other benefits it might bring to himself or to persons he cared for.

We now have an answer to the question what sort of proof the principle of utility admits of. Suppose the opinion I have stated is psychologically true: human nature is so constituted that it desires nothing that is not either a part of happiness or a means to happiness. Then we can have no other proof, and we need none, that these are the only things desirable. If so, happiness is the sole end of human action, and promoting it is the test by which all human conduct is to be judged. It necessarily follows that happiness must be the criterion of morality, since a part is included in the whole.

And now we must decide whether this is really so: whether mankind desire nothing for itself except what is a pleasure to them, or what they feel the absence of as a pain. We have evidently arrived at a question of fact and experience, which depends, like all similar questions, on evidence. It can be determined only by practiced self-consciousness and self-observation, assisted by observation of others. I believe that these sources of evidence, impartially consulted, will declare that desiring a thing and finding it pleasant, and being averse to it and thinking of it as painful, are entirely inseparable phenomena, or rather two parts of the same phenomenon. In strictness of language they are two different ways of naming the same psychological fact. To think of an object as desirable (unless for the sake of its consequences) and to think of it as pleasant are one and the same thing. And to desire anything, except in proportion as the idea of it is pleasant, is a physical and metaphysical impossibility.

To me this is so obvious that I expect it will hardly be disputed. The objection raised will be, not that desire can possibly be directed ultimately to anything except pleasure and exemption from pain, but that the will is a different thing from desire. It will be said that a person of confirmed virtue, or any other person whose purposes are fixed, carries out his purposes without any thought of the pleasure he has in contemplating them, or expects to get from their fulfillment. He persists in acting on them even though these pleasures are much diminished, by changes in his character or by decay of his passive sensibilities, or are outweighed by the pains that the pursuit of the purposes may bring on him. All this I fully admit, and I have stated it elsewhere as positively and emphatically as anyone. Will, the active phenomenon, is a different thing from desire, the state of passive sensibility. Though it was originally an offshoot from desire, it may in time take root and detach itself from the parent stock. So much so that in the case of a habitual purpose, instead of willing the thing because we desire it, we often desire it only because we will it. This, however, is but an instance of that familiar fact, the power of habit, and is in no way confined to virtuous actions. Many indifferent things that men originally did from a motive of some sort, they continue to do from habit. Sometimes this is done unconsciously, the consciousness coming only after the action. At other times it is done with conscious volition, but volition that has become habitual and is put into operation by the force of habit, perhaps in opposition to the deliberate preference, as often happens with those who have contracted habits of vicious or hurtful indulgence. Third and last comes the case in which the habitual act of will in the individual instance is not in contradiction to the general intention prevailing at other times but in fulfillment of it. That is the case of the person of confirmed virtue, and of all who pursue any determinate end deliberately and consistently. The distinction between will and desire, understood in this way, is an authentic and highly important psychological fact. But the fact consists solely in this: will, like all other parts of our constitution, is amenable to habit, and we may will from habit what we no longer desire for itself, or desire only because we will it. It is not the less true that will, in the beginning, is entirely produced by desire, including in that term the repelling influence of pain as well as the attractive one of pleasure. Let us consider no longer the person who has a confirmed will to do right, but him in whom that virtuous will is still feeble, conquerable by temptation, and not to be fully relied on. By what means can it be strengthened? How can the will to be virtuous, where it does not exist in sufficient force, be implanted or awakened? Only by making the person _desire_ virtue, by making him think of it in a pleasurable light, or of its absence in a painful one. It is by associating the doing of right with pleasure, or the doing of wrong with pain, or by eliciting, impressing and bringing home to the person's experience the pleasure naturally involved in the one or the pain in the other, that it is possible to call forth that will to be virtuous. When confirmed, that will acts without any thought of either pleasure or pain. Will is the child of desire, and passes out of the dominion of its parent only to come under that of habit. What is the result of habit gives no presumption of being intrinsically good. And there would be no reason for wishing that the purpose of virtue should become independent of pleasure and pain, were it not that the pleasurable and painful associations that prompt to virtue cannot be sufficiently depended on for unerring constancy of action until habit has supported them. Both in feeling and in conduct, habit is the only thing that imparts certainty. It is because it matters to others to be able to rely absolutely on one's feelings and conduct, and matters to oneself to be able to rely on one's own, that the will to do right ought to be cultivated into this habitual independence. In other words, this state of the will is a means to good, not intrinsically a good. It does not contradict the doctrine that nothing is a good to human beings except in so far as it is either itself pleasurable, or a means of attaining pleasure or averting pain.
But if this doctrine is true, the principle of utility is proved. Whether it is true or not must now be left to the consideration of the thoughtful reader.

chapters.title: Chapter 5 — On the Connection Between Justice and Utility
paragraphs: Throughout the history of speculation, one of the strongest obstacles to accepting the doctrine that Utility or Happiness is the criterion of right and wrong has come from the idea of Justice. That word calls up a powerful sentiment and an apparently clear perception, with a speed and certainty like instinct. To most thinkers these have seemed to point to a quality inherent in things. They seem to show that the Just must exist in Nature as something absolute, generically distinct from every variety of the Expedient, and in idea opposed to it — though (as is commonly acknowledged) never, in the long run, separated from it in fact.

With this moral sentiment, as with our others, the question of its origin is not necessarily connected with the question of its binding force. That Nature has given us a feeling does not by itself justify everything the feeling urges. The feeling of justice might be a peculiar instinct and yet need, like our other instincts, to be controlled and enlightened by a higher reason. We have intellectual instincts, which lead us to judge in a particular way, as well as animal instincts, which prompt us to act in a particular way. There is no necessity that the former be more infallible in their sphere than the latter in theirs. Wrong judgments may occasionally be suggested by the one just as wrong actions are by the other. But it is one thing to believe that we have natural feelings of justice, and another to accept them as an ultimate criterion of conduct. Even so, in point of fact, these two opinions are very closely connected. Mankind are always predisposed to believe that any subjective feeling which cannot be accounted for in some other way is a revelation of some objective reality. Our present object is to determine whether the reality to which the feeling of justice corresponds is one that needs any such special revelation. Is the justice or injustice of an action something intrinsically peculiar, distinct from all its other qualities? Or is it only a combination of certain of those qualities, seen under a peculiar aspect? For this inquiry it is practically important to ask whether the feeling of justice and injustice is itself _sui generis_, like our sensations of color and taste, or is a derivative feeling, formed by a combination of others. It is all the more essential to examine this because people are in general willing enough to allow that, objectively, the dictates of justice coincide with a part of the field of General Expediency. But the subjective mental feeling of Justice differs from the feeling that commonly attaches to simple expediency, and, except in extreme cases of the latter, it is far more imperative in its demands. So people find it difficult to see in Justice only a particular kind or branch of general utility, and they think that its superior binding force requires a totally different origin.

To throw light on this question, we must try to find out what distinguishes justice or injustice. What quality is attributed in common to all modes of conduct that are called unjust, and sets them apart from modes of conduct that are disapproved but are not given that particular epithet of disapprobation? (Or is there no such quality at all? For justice, like many other moral attributes, is best defined by its opposite.) Suppose that some one common attribute, or collection of attributes, is always present in everything that men are accustomed to call just or unjust. Then we may judge whether this attribute, or combination of attributes, could gather round it a sentiment of that peculiar character and intensity by virtue of the general laws of our emotional constitution. Or we may judge whether the sentiment is inexplicable and must be regarded as a special provision of Nature. If we find the former to be the case, then in settling this question we shall also have settled the main problem. If the latter, we shall have to look for some other way of investigating it.

To find what a variety of objects have in common, we must start by looking at the objects themselves, one by one. So let us go in turn through the various kinds of action, and the arrangements of human affairs, that universal or widely shared opinion classes as Just or Unjust. The things known to arouse the sentiments tied to those names are very many and very different. I shall run through them quickly, without studying any particular order.

First, it is mostly considered unjust to take from anyone his personal liberty, his property, or any other thing that is his by law. So here we have one use of the terms just and unjust in a perfectly definite sense: to respect the _legal rights_ of anyone is just, and to violate them is unjust. But this judgment has several exceptions, which come from the other forms that the notions of justice and injustice take. For example, the person deprived may (as the phrase is) have _forfeited_ the rights he loses. We shall come back to that case shortly. But there is also this:

Secondly: the legal rights of which he is deprived may be rights that _ought_ not to have belonged to him. In other words, the law that confers these rights on him may be a bad law. When it is so, or when (which is the same thing for our purpose) it is supposed to be so, opinions will differ about the justice or injustice of infringing it. Some maintain that no law, however bad, ought to be disobeyed by an individual citizen. If he opposes it at all, he should do so only by trying to get it altered by competent authority. Those who hold this opinion defend it on grounds of expediency, principally the importance, to the common interest of mankind, of keeping inviolate the sentiment of submission to law. (The opinion condemns many of the most illustrious benefactors of mankind. It would often protect pernicious institutions against the only weapons which, in the state of things existing at the time, have any chance of succeeding against them.) Other persons hold the directly contrary opinion: any law judged to be bad may blamelessly be disobeyed, even if it is not judged to be unjust but only inexpedient. Others again would confine the license of disobedience to unjust laws. But then some say that all laws which are inexpedient are unjust, since every law imposes some restriction on the natural liberty of mankind, and that restriction is an injustice unless it is legitimated by tending to their good. Amid these diversities of opinion, it seems to be universally admitted that there may be unjust laws. Law, consequently, is not the ultimate criterion of justice, and it may give one person a benefit, or impose on another an evil, which justice condemns. When, however, a law is thought to be unjust, it always seems to be regarded as unjust in the same way that a breach of law is unjust, namely by infringing somebody's right. In this case that right cannot be a legal right, so it receives a different name and is called a moral right. We may say, therefore, that a second case of injustice consists in taking from any person, or withholding from him, that to which he has a _moral right_.

Thirdly, everyone considers it just that a person receive what he _deserves_, whether good or evil, and unjust that he receive a good, or be made to suffer an evil, that he does not deserve. This is perhaps the clearest and most emphatic form in which people in general conceive justice. Because it involves the notion of desert, we are led to ask what makes up desert. Speaking generally, a person is understood to deserve good if he does right, and evil if he does wrong. In a more particular sense, he is understood to deserve good from those to whom he does or has done good, and evil from those to whom he does or has done evil. Returning good for evil has never been regarded as fulfilling justice. It is regarded as a case where the claims of justice are set aside out of obedience to other considerations.

Fourthly, everyone admits that it is unjust to _break faith_ with anyone, that is, to violate an engagement, express or implied, or to disappoint expectations that our own conduct has raised, at least where we raised them knowingly and voluntarily. Like the other obligations of justice just mentioned, this one is not regarded as absolute. A stronger obligation of justice on the other side can overrule it. So can the conduct of the person concerned, if it is deemed to free us from our obligation to him and to make him _forfeit_ the benefit he was led to expect.

Fifthly, by universal admission, it is inconsistent with justice to be _partial_: to show favor or preference to one person over another in matters to which favor and preference do not properly apply. Impartiality, however, does not seem to be regarded as a duty in itself. It seems rather to be instrumental to some other duty. For it is admitted that favor and preference are not always censurable, and indeed the cases in which they are condemned are the exception rather than the rule. A person would be more likely to be blamed than applauded for giving his family or friends no superiority in good offices over strangers, when he could do so without violating any other duty. And no one thinks it unjust to seek one person in preference to another as a friend, connection, or companion. Impartiality where rights are concerned is of course obligatory, but this is included in the more general obligation of giving everyone his right. A tribunal, for example, must be impartial, because it is bound to award a disputed object, without regard to any other consideration, to whichever of the two parties has the right to it. In other cases impartiality means being influenced solely by desert, as with those who administer reward and punishment as such, in the capacity of judges, teachers, or parents. In others it means being influenced solely by consideration for the public interest, as in choosing among candidates for a Government employment. In short, impartiality as an obligation of justice may be said to mean being influenced exclusively by the considerations which are supposed to be the ones that ought to influence the particular case in hand, and resisting the pull of any motives that prompt conduct different from what those considerations would dictate.

Closely allied to impartiality is the idea of _equality_. It often enters as a component into both the conception and the practice of justice, and many people see it as the essence of justice. But here, even more than elsewhere, different people hold different notions of justice, and the variations always follow their notion of utility. Each person holds that equality is what justice dictates, unless he thinks expediency calls for inequality. Even the defenders of the most outrageous inequality in the rights themselves maintain that the rights of all deserve equal protection. Even in slave countries it is admitted in theory that the slave's rights, such as they are, ought to be as sacred as the master's, and that a tribunal which enforces them less strictly is lacking in justice. Yet institutions that leave the slave hardly any rights to enforce are not deemed unjust, because they are not deemed inexpedient. People who think utility requires distinctions of rank see no injustice in an unequal distribution of riches and social privileges. People who think that inequality inexpedient think it unjust too. Whoever thinks government necessary sees no injustice in the inequality created when a magistrate is given powers that other people lack. Even among the holders of levelling doctrines there are as many questions of justice as there are differences of opinion about expediency. Some Communists consider it unjust to share the produce of the community's labor on any principle but exact equality. Others think it just that those with the greatest needs receive most. Others hold that those who work harder, or produce more, or give more valuable service to the community, may justly claim a larger share of the produce. And the sense of natural justice can plausibly be called on in support of every one of these opinions.

The term Justice is applied in so many diverse ways, and yet it is not regarded as ambiguous. It is therefore somewhat difficult to grasp the mental link that holds these applications together, the link on which the moral sentiment attached to the term essentially depends. Perhaps, in this difficulty, we may get some help from the history of the word, as its etymology indicates it.

In most languages, if not in all, the etymology of the word corresponding to Just points to an origin connected either with positive law or with what was in most cases the primitive form of law, authoritative custom. _Justum_ is a form of _jussum_, that which has been ordered. _Jus_ has the same origin. _Dichanou_ comes from _dichae_, whose principal meaning, at least in the historical ages of Greece, was a suit at law. Originally, indeed, it meant only the mode or _manner_ of doing things, but it early came to mean the _prescribed_ manner: that which the recognized authorities, patriarchal, judicial, or political, would enforce. _Recht_, from which came _right_ and _righteous_, is synonymous with law. The original meaning of _recht_, indeed, did not point to law but to physical straightness, just as _wrong_ and its Latin equivalents meant twisted or tortuous. From this it is argued that right did not originally mean law, but that on the contrary law meant right. However that may be, _recht_ and _droit_ became restricted in their meaning to positive law, although much that is not required by law is equally necessary to moral straightness or rectitude. That fact is as significant of the original character of moral ideas as if the derivation had run the other way. The courts of justice and the administration of justice are the courts and the administration of law. _La justice_, in French, is the established term for judicature. There can, I think, be no doubt that the _idée mère_, the primitive element, in forming the notion of justice was conformity to law. Among the Hebrews, up to the birth of Christianity, it constituted the entire idea. This might be expected of a people whose laws tried to embrace every subject on which precepts were required, and who believed those laws to be a direct emanation from the Supreme Being. But other nations, in particular the Greeks and Romans, knew that their laws had been made originally by men, and were still being made by men. They were not afraid to admit that those men might make bad laws. Men might do by law the very same things, from the same motives, which would be called unjust if individuals did them without the sanction of law. And hence the sentiment of injustice came to be attached not to all violations of law, but only to violations of such laws as _ought_ to exist, including such as ought to exist but do not, and to laws themselves if they were supposed to be contrary to what ought to be law. In this way the idea of law and of its injunctions remained predominant in the notion of justice, even when the laws actually in force ceased to be accepted as its standard.

It is true that mankind consider the idea of justice and its obligations applicable to many things which are not regulated by law, and which no one desires to have regulated by law. Nobody wants laws to interfere with the whole detail of private life. Yet everyone allows that in all daily conduct a person may show himself to be just or unjust, and does so. But even here, the idea of the breach of what ought to be law still lingers in a modified shape. It would always give us pleasure, and chime in with our feelings of fitness, if acts which we deem unjust were punished, though we do not always think it expedient for the tribunals to do the punishing. We forgo that gratification on account of incidental inconveniences. We should be glad to see just conduct enforced and injustice repressed, even in the minutest details, if we were not (with reason) afraid of trusting the magistrate with so unlimited an amount of power over individuals. When we think that a person is bound in justice to do a thing, it is an ordinary form of language to say that he ought to be compelled to do it. We should be gratified to see the obligation enforced by anybody who had the power. If we see that enforcing it by law would be inexpedient, we lament the impossibility. We consider the impunity given to injustice an evil, and we try to make amends for it by bringing a strong expression of our own and the public disapprobation to bear on the offender. Thus the idea of legal constraint is still the generating idea of the notion of justice. That idea goes through several transformations before the notion, as it exists in an advanced state of society, is complete.

The above is, I think, a true account, as far as it goes, of the origin and progressive growth of the idea of justice. But we must observe that as yet it contains nothing to distinguish that obligation from moral obligation in general. For the truth is that the idea of penal sanction, which is the essence of law, enters not only into the conception of injustice but into that of any kind of wrong. We do not call anything wrong unless we mean to imply that a person ought to be punished in some way for doing it: if not by law, then by the opinion of his fellow creatures; if not by opinion, then by the reproaches of his own conscience. This seems the real turning point of the distinction between morality and simple expediency. It is a part of the notion of Duty, in every one of its forms, that a person may rightfully be compelled to fulfill it. Duty is a thing which may be _exacted_ from a person, as one exacts a debt. Unless we think that it might be exacted from him, we do not call it his duty. Reasons of prudence, or the interest of other people, may count against actually exacting it. But it is clearly understood that the person himself would not be entitled to complain. There are other things, on the contrary, which we wish people to do, which we like or admire them for doing, and perhaps dislike or despise them for not doing, but which we admit they are not bound to do. This is not a case of moral obligation. We do not blame them, that is, we do not think that they are proper objects of punishment. How we come by these ideas of deserving and not deserving punishment will appear, perhaps, in what follows. But I think there is no doubt that this distinction lies at the bottom of the notions of right and wrong. We call any conduct wrong, or use instead some other term of dislike or disparagement, according as we think that the person ought or ought not to be punished for it. And we say that it would be right to do so and so, or merely that it would be desirable or laudable, according as we would wish to see the person it concerns compelled, or only persuaded and exhorted, to act in that manner.[C]

This, then, is the characteristic difference that marks off morality in general (not justice) from the remaining provinces of Expediency and Worthiness. We must still look for the character that distinguishes justice from other branches of morality. Now it is known that ethical writers divide moral duties into two classes, which they denote by the ill-chosen expressions duties of perfect and of imperfect obligation. In the latter, though the act is obligatory, the particular occasions of performing it are left to our choice. Charity or beneficence is an example: we are indeed bound to practice it, but not toward any definite person, nor at any prescribed time. In the more precise language of philosophic jurists, duties of perfect obligation are those by virtue of which a correlative right resides in some person or persons. Duties of imperfect obligation are those moral obligations which do not give birth to any right. I think it will be found that this distinction exactly coincides with the one between justice and the other obligations of morality. In our survey of the various popular acceptations of justice, the term generally appeared to involve the idea of a personal right: a claim on the part of one or more individuals, like the claim the law gives when it confers a proprietary or other legal right. The injustice may consist in depriving a person of a possession, or in breaking faith with him, or in treating him worse than he deserves, or worse than other people who have no greater claims. In each case the supposition implies two things: a wrong done, and some assignable person who is wronged. Injustice may also be done by treating a person better than others, but then the wrong is to his competitors, who are also assignable persons. It seems to me that this feature of the case, a right in some person correlative to the moral obligation, constitutes the specific difference between justice and generosity or beneficence. Justice implies something which it is not only right to do and wrong not to do, but which some individual person can claim from us as his moral right. No one has a moral right to our generosity or beneficence, because we are not morally bound to practice those virtues toward any given individual. And it will be found, here as with every correct definition, that the instances which seem to conflict with it are those which most confirm it. Suppose a moralist tries, as some have done, to make out that mankind generally, though not any given individual, have a right to all the good we can do them. By that thesis he at once includes generosity and beneficence within the category of justice. He is obliged to say that our utmost exertions are due to our fellow creatures, thus assimilating them to a debt; or that nothing less can be a sufficient _return_ for what society does for us, thus classing the case as one of gratitude. Both of these are acknowledged cases of justice. Wherever there is a right, the case is one of justice and not of the virtue of beneficence. And whoever does not place the distinction between justice and morality in general where we have now placed it will be found to make no distinction between them at all, but to merge all morality in justice.

We have now tried to determine the distinctive elements that enter into the composition of the idea of justice. We are ready to inquire whether the feeling that accompanies the idea is attached to it by a special dispensation of nature, or whether it could have grown up out of the idea itself, by any known laws. In particular, we must ask whether it can have originated in considerations of general expediency.

I hold that the sentiment itself does not come from anything that would commonly, or correctly, be called an idea of expediency. Whatever is moral in the sentiment does come from it, though the sentiment itself does not.

We have seen that the sentiment of justice has two essential ingredients. One is the desire to punish a person who has done harm. The other is the knowledge or belief that some definite individual or individuals have been harmed.

Now it appears to me that the desire to punish a person who has harmed some individual grows up spontaneously out of two sentiments, both in the highest degree natural, which either are instincts or resemble them: the impulse of self-defense and the feeling of sympathy.

It is natural to resent, and to repel or retaliate, any harm done or attempted against ourselves or against those with whom we sympathize. We need not discuss here the origin of this sentiment. Whether it is an instinct or a result of intelligence, we know that it is common to all animal nature, for every animal tries to hurt those who have hurt it, or who it thinks are about to hurt it or its young. Human beings differ from other animals on this point in only two particulars. First, they are capable of sympathizing not solely with their offspring or, like some of the more noble animals, with some superior animal who is kind to them, but with all human beings, and even with all sentient beings. Secondly, they have a more developed intelligence, which gives a wider range to the whole of their sentiments, whether self-regarding or sympathetic. By virtue of his superior intelligence, even apart from his wider range of sympathy, a human being can apprehend a community of interest between himself and the human society of which he forms a part. Because of this, any conduct that threatens the security of society generally threatens his own, and calls forth his instinct (if instinct it be) of self-defense. The same superiority of intelligence, joined to the power of sympathizing with human beings generally, enables him to attach himself to the collective idea of his tribe, his country, or mankind, in such a manner that any act hurtful to them rouses his instinct of sympathy and urges him to resistance.

The sentiment of justice, in the element of it that consists of the desire to punish, is thus, I conceive, the natural feeling of retaliation or vengeance. Intellect and sympathy make it applicable to those injuries, that is, to those hurts, which wound us through, or in common with, society at large. This sentiment, in itself, has nothing moral in it. What is moral is its exclusive subordination to the social sympathies, so that it waits on their call and obeys it. For the natural feeling tends to make us resent indiscriminately whatever anyone does that is disagreeable to us. But when it is moralized by the social feeling, it acts only in directions conformable to the general good. Just persons resent a hurt to society, though it is not otherwise a hurt to themselves. And they do not resent a hurt to themselves, however painful, unless it is of the kind which society has a common interest with them in repressing.

It is no objection to this doctrine to say that when we feel our sentiment of justice outraged, we are not thinking of society at large, or of any collective interest, but only of the individual case. It is common enough, certainly, though the reverse of commendable, to feel resentment merely because we have suffered pain. But consider a person whose resentment is really a moral feeling, that is, who considers whether an act is blameable before he allows himself to resent it. Such a person may not say expressly to himself that he is standing up for the interest of society, but he certainly does feel that he is asserting a rule which is for the benefit of others as well as for his own. If he is not feeling this, and is regarding the act solely as it affects him individually, he is not consciously just: he is not concerning himself about the justice of his actions. Even anti-utilitarian moralists admit this. When Kant (as remarked before) propounds as the fundamental principle of morals, "So act, that thy rule of conduct might be adopted as a law by all rational beings," he virtually acknowledges that the interest of mankind collectively, or at least of mankind indiscriminately, must be in the mind of the agent when he is conscientiously deciding on the morality of the act. Otherwise he uses words without a meaning. For it cannot even be plausibly maintained that even a rule of utter selfishness could not _possibly_ be adopted by all rational beings, or that there is any insuperable obstacle in the nature of things to its adoption. To give any meaning to Kant's principle, the sense put on it must be that we ought to shape our conduct by a rule which all rational beings might adopt _with benefit to their collective interest_.

To sum up: the idea of justice involves two things, a rule of conduct and a sentiment that sanctions the rule. We must suppose the rule to be shared by all mankind and meant for their good. The sentiment is a desire that anyone who breaks the rule should be punished. The idea also brings in the conception of some definite person who is harmed by the violation, and whose rights (to use the expression suited to the case) it violates. As I see it, the sentiment of justice is the animal desire to hit back at a hurt or damage done to oneself, or to those with whom one sympathizes, extended to cover all persons by two things: the human capacity for enlarged sympathy and the human conception of intelligent self-interest. The feeling owes its morality to these two human elements, and owes its peculiar impressiveness and energy of self-assertion to the animal desire.

All along I have treated the idea of a _right_, held by the injured person and violated by the injury, as no separate ingredient of the idea and sentiment of justice. It is one of the forms in which the other two elements present themselves. Those elements are a hurt to some assignable person or persons, and a demand for punishment. I think that if we examine our own minds we will find these two things cover all we mean by the violation of a right. To call something a person's right is to say that he has a valid claim on society to protect him in having it, whether by the force of law or by education and opinion. If we judge his claim sufficient, for whatever reason, to have something guaranteed to him by society, we say he has a right to it. If we want to prove that something is not his by right, we count that done once it is admitted that society ought not to take steps to secure it to him, and should leave it to chance or to his own efforts. So a person is said to have a right to whatever he can earn in fair professional competition, since society ought not to let anyone else prevent him from trying to earn as much as he can in that way. But he has no right to three hundred a year, even if he happens to be earning it, since society is not called on to make sure that he earns that sum. If, on the other hand, he owns ten thousand pounds in three per cent stock, he _has_ a right to three hundred a year, since society has taken on an obligation to provide him with an income of that amount.

To have a right, then, is, I hold, to have something that society ought to defend me in possessing. Suppose the objector goes on to ask why society ought to do so. I can give him no reason but general utility. Suppose that expression does not seem to convey enough of the strength of the obligation, or to explain the peculiar energy of the feeling. If so, the cause is that the sentiment is composed of an animal element, the thirst for retaliation, as well as a rational one. That thirst draws its intensity, and its moral justification, from the extraordinarily important and impressive kind of utility at stake. The interest concerned is security, which everyone feels to be the most vital of all interests. Almost every other earthly benefit is needed by one person and not by another, and many can, if necessary, be cheerfully done without, or replaced by something else. Security, however, no human being can possibly do without. All our immunity from evil depends on it, as does the whole value of every good beyond the passing moment. For if whoever was momentarily stronger than we are could take everything from us the next instant, nothing but the gratification of the instant would be worth anything to us. Now this most indispensable of all necessaries, after physical nutriment, cannot be had unless the machinery that provides it is kept constantly at work. So we claim that our fellow creatures must join in making the very groundwork of our existence safe for us. Feelings gather around this claim that are far more intense than those in any of the more common cases of utility, and so the difference in degree (as often happens in psychology) becomes a real difference in kind. The claim acquires that character of absoluteness, that apparent infinity, that incommensurability with every other consideration, which marks the difference between the feeling of right and wrong and the feeling of ordinary expediency and inexpediency. These feelings are so powerful, and we count so positively on a responsive feeling in others (since all are alike interested), that _ought_ and _should_ grow into _must_. Recognized indispensability becomes a moral necessity, like a physical one, and often equal to it in binding force.

Suppose the analysis I have given, or something like it, is not the right account of the notion of justice. Suppose justice is quite independent of utility and is a standard _per se_, which the mind can recognize by simply looking into itself. Then it is hard to see why that internal oracle should be so ambiguous, or why so many things look just or unjust depending on how they are viewed. We are constantly told that Utility is an uncertain standard, which every person interprets differently, and that safety lies only in the immutable, ineffaceable and unmistakable dictates of Justice, which carry their own evidence and do not fluctuate with opinion. From this one would suppose that questions of justice could give rise to no controversy, and that if we take justice for our rule, applying it to a given case would leave as little doubt as a mathematical demonstration. The fact is far otherwise. People differ as much, and argue as fiercely, about what is just as about what is useful to society. Nations and individuals differ in their notions of justice. And even in the mind of one individual, justice is not a single rule, principle or maxim but many, which do not always agree in what they dictate. In choosing among them he is guided either by some extraneous standard or by his own personal predilections.

Some people say, for instance, that it is unjust to punish anyone as an example to others, and that punishment is just only when it is meant for the good of the person punished. Others take the extreme opposite view. They contend that punishing adults for their own benefit is despotism and injustice, because if the matter at issue is solely their own good, no one has a right to override their own judgment of it. Such persons, they say, may justly be punished to prevent evil to others, since this is an exercise of the legitimate right of self-defense. Mr. Owen, again, affirms that it is unjust to punish at all. The criminal did not make his own character: his education and the circumstances around him made him a criminal, and he is not responsible for those. All these opinions are extremely plausible. As long as the question is argued purely as one of justice, without going down to the principles beneath justice that are the source of its authority, I cannot see how any of these reasoners can be refuted. For each of the three builds on rules of justice that are admittedly true. The first appeals to the acknowledged injustice of picking out an individual and sacrificing him, without his consent, for the benefit of others. The second relies on the acknowledged justice of self-defense, and on the admitted injustice of forcing one person to conform to another's notions of what his good consists in. The Owenite invokes the admitted principle that it is unjust to punish anyone for what he cannot help. Each triumphs as long as he is not forced to consider any maxim of justice except the one he has chosen. But once their maxims are brought face to face, each disputant seems to have just as much to say for himself as the others do. None of them can carry out his own notion of justice without trampling on another that binds equally. These are difficulties. They have always been felt to be so, and many devices have been invented to sidestep them rather than overcome them. To escape the last of the three, men imagined what they called the freedom of the will. They fancied that a man whose will is in a thoroughly hateful state could not be justly punished unless that state of his will was supposed to have arisen without any influence from earlier circumstances. To escape the other difficulties, a favorite contrivance has been the fiction of a contract. At some unknown time, it says, all the members of society agreed to obey the laws and consented to be punished for disobeying them. Thereby, it is assumed, they gave their legislators a right to punish them, whether for their own good or for society's, which the legislators would not otherwise have had. This happy thought was taken to dispose of the whole difficulty, and to justify inflicting punishment by another received maxim of justice, _volenti non fit injuria_: what is done with the consent of the person supposed to be hurt by it is not unjust. I hardly need remark that even if the consent were not a mere fiction, this maxim has no more authority than the others it is brought in to displace. It is, on the contrary, an instructive specimen of the loose and irregular way in which supposed principles of justice grow up. Evidently this one came into use to serve the coarse exigencies of courts of law. Courts are sometimes obliged to be content with very uncertain presumptions, because of the greater evils that would often follow if they tried to cut finer. Yet even courts of law cannot keep to the maxim consistently, for they allow voluntary engagements to be set aside for fraud, and sometimes for mere mistake or misinformation.

Again, once it is admitted that inflicting punishment is legitimate, discussion of how to match punishment to offenses brings many conflicting conceptions of justice to light. No rule appeals so strongly to the primitive and spontaneous sentiment of justice as the _lex talionis_, an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth. Europe has generally given up this principle of Jewish and Muslim law as a practical maxim. Still, I suspect that most minds secretly hanker after it. When retribution happens to strike an offender in exactly that shape, the general satisfaction people show proves how natural is the sentiment to which this repayment in kind is welcome. For many people the test of justice in penal infliction is that the punishment should be proportioned to the offense. They mean that it should be measured exactly by the culprit's moral guilt (whatever their standard for measuring moral guilt may be). On their view, how much punishment is needed to deter from the offense has nothing to do with justice. There are others for whom that consideration is everything. They maintain that it is not just, at least for man, to inflict on a fellow creature, whatever his offenses, any suffering beyond the least that will keep him from repeating his misconduct and others from imitating it.

Here is another example, from a subject already touched on once. In a co-operative industrial association, is it just or not for talent or skill to earn higher pay? Those who say no argue that whoever does his best deserves equally well, and in justice should not be placed in an inferior position through no fault of his own. Superior abilities, they say, already have more than enough advantages in the admiration they excite, the personal influence they command and the inner satisfactions that go with them, without also receiving a larger share of the world's goods. They add that society is bound in justice to compensate the less favored for this undeserved inequality of advantages rather than to make it worse. Those who say yes contend that society gets more from the more efficient laborer. His services being more useful, they say, society owes him a larger return. A greater share of the joint result is actually his work, and refusing his claim to it is a kind of robbery. If he is to receive no more than others, then he can justly be required to produce no more, and to give less time and exertion in proportion to his greater efficiency. Who is to decide between these appeals to conflicting principles of justice? In this case justice has two sides that cannot be brought into harmony, and the two disputants have taken opposite sides. One looks at what it is just for the individual to receive, the other at what it is just for the community to give. Each, from his own point of view, cannot be answered, and any choice between them on grounds of justice must be perfectly arbitrary. Social utility alone can decide the preference.

How many, again, and how irreconcilable, are the standards of justice cited in debating how taxes should be shared out. One opinion is that payment to the State should be in numerical proportion to pecuniary means. Others think that justice demands what they call graduated taxation, which takes a higher percentage from those who have more to spare. In point of natural justice, a strong case could be made for ignoring means altogether and taking the same absolute sum from everyone (wherever it could be got), just as the members of a mess or a club all pay the same sum for the same privileges, whether or not they can equally afford it. It might be said that law and government protect everyone and are needed equally by everyone, so there is no injustice in making everyone buy that protection at the same price. We reckon it justice, not injustice, for a dealer to charge all customers the same price for the same article, rather than a price that varies with their means of payment. Applied to taxation, this doctrine finds no advocates, because it conflicts strongly with men's feelings of humanity and their perceptions of social expediency. Yet the principle of justice it invokes is as true and as binding as those that can be set against it. So it quietly shapes the defense offered for other ways of assessing taxes. People feel obliged to argue that the State does more for the rich than for the poor, to justify taking more from the rich. This is in reality not true. Without law or government the rich would be far better able to protect themselves than the poor, and would probably succeed in turning the poor into their slaves. Others, again, defer to the same conception of justice enough to maintain that everyone should pay an equal capitation tax for the protection of their persons (which are of equal value to all), and an unequal tax for the protection of their property, which is unequal. Others reply to this that the all of one man is as valuable to him as the all of another. There is no way out of these confusions except the utilitarian.

Is the difference between the Just and the Expedient, then, merely an imaginary distinction? Have mankind been deluded in thinking justice a more sacred thing than policy, and in thinking that policy should be heeded only after justice has been satisfied? By no means. The account we have given of the nature and origin of the sentiment recognizes a real distinction. Not even those who profess the most sublime contempt for the consequences of actions, as an element in their morality, attach more importance to this distinction than I do. I dispute the claims of any theory that sets up an imaginary standard of justice not grounded on utility. But I regard the justice that is grounded on utility as the chief part of all morality, and incomparably its most sacred and binding part. Justice is a name for certain classes of moral rules. These bear more closely on the essentials of human well-being, and are therefore more absolutely obligatory, than any other rules for guiding life. The notion we found to be of the essence of the idea of justice, that of a right held by an individual, implies and bears witness to this more binding obligation.

The moral rules that forbid mankind to hurt one another (and we must never forget that this includes wrongful interference with each other's freedom) are more vital to human well-being than any maxims, however important, that merely point out the best way to manage some department of human affairs. They also have this peculiarity: they are the main element in determining all the social feelings of mankind. Only their observance preserves peace among human beings. If obeying them were not the rule and disobeying them the exception, everyone would see in everyone else a probable enemy, against whom he would have to guard himself perpetually. What is hardly less important, these are the precepts that mankind have the strongest and most direct motives to impress upon one another. By merely giving each other prudential instruction or exhortation, they may gain nothing, or think they gain nothing. In teaching each other the duty of positive beneficence they have an unmistakable interest, but a far smaller one: a person may possibly not need the benefits others can give, but he always needs them not to do him hurt. So the moralities that protect each individual from being harmed by others, either directly or by being hindered in his freedom to pursue his own good, are at once those he himself has most at heart and those he has the strongest interest in publishing and enforcing by word and deed. A person's observance of these tests and decides his fitness to exist as one of the fellowship of human beings, for it determines whether he is a nuisance to those he comes in contact with. Now it is these moralities, primarily, that make up the obligations of justice. The most marked cases of injustice, which set the tone of the feeling of repugnance that characterizes the sentiment, are acts of wrongful aggression or wrongful exercise of power over someone. The next most marked are those of wrongfully withholding from him something that is his due. In both cases the wrong is to inflict a positive hurt on him, either as direct suffering or as the lack of some good that he had reasonable ground, whether physical or social, to count on.

The same powerful motives that command the observance of these primary moralities also require the punishment of those who violate them. Self-defense, the defense of others and vengeance are all called forth against such persons. Retribution, or evil for evil, therefore becomes closely connected with the sentiment of justice, and is universally included in the idea. Good for good is also one of the dictates of justice. Its social utility is evident, and it carries a natural human feeling with it. At first sight, though, it lacks the obvious connection with hurt or injury that exists in the most elementary cases of just and unjust, and that is the source of the characteristic intensity of the sentiment. But the connection, though less obvious, is just as real. Someone who accepts benefits and refuses a return when it is needed does a real hurt. He disappoints one of the most natural and reasonable of expectations, one he must at least tacitly have encouraged, since otherwise the benefits would seldom have been given. How important the disappointment of expectation is among human evils and wrongs can be seen from the fact that it makes up the principal criminality of two such highly immoral acts as a breach of friendship and a breach of promise. Few hurts a human being can suffer are greater, and none wounds more, than to have that fail him in his hour of need on which he habitually and with full assurance relied. Few wrongs are greater than this mere withholding of good, and none arouses more resentment, whether in the sufferer or in a sympathizing spectator. The principle, then, of giving to each what they deserve, that is, good for good as well as evil for evil, is not only contained in the idea of Justice as we have defined it. It is also a proper object of that intensity of sentiment which places the Just, in human estimation, above the merely Expedient.

Most of the maxims of justice that are current in the world and commonly appealed to in its dealings are simply means of carrying out the principles of justice we have just described. Some examples: a person is responsible only for what he has done voluntarily or could voluntarily have avoided; it is unjust to condemn anyone without a hearing; the punishment ought to be proportioned to the offense; and the like. These maxims are meant to keep the just principle of evil for evil from being twisted into the infliction of evil without that justification. Most of these common maxims came into use through the practice of courts of justice. Courts were naturally led to recognize and work out, more fully than others were likely to do, the rules they need to perform their double function of inflicting punishment when it is due and awarding each person his right.

Impartiality, the first of judicial virtues, is an obligation of justice, partly for the reason just given: it is a necessary condition for fulfilling the other obligations of justice. But that is not the only source of the exalted rank, among human obligations, of the maxims of equality and impartiality, which both popular opinion and the most enlightened opinion include among the precepts of justice. From one point of view they can be regarded as corollaries of the principles already laid down. If it is a duty to give each according to his deserts, returning good for good as well as repressing evil by evil, then we must necessarily treat equally well (when no higher duty forbids) all who have deserved equally well of us. It follows too that society should treat equally well all who have deserved equally well of it, that is, who have deserved equally well absolutely. This is the highest abstract standard of social and distributive justice. All institutions, and the efforts of all virtuous citizens, should be made to converge on it as far as possible. But this great moral duty rests on a still deeper foundation. It flows directly from the first principle of morals, and is not a mere logical corollary of secondary or derivative doctrines. It is involved in the very meaning of Utility, or the Greatest-Happiness Principle. Unless one person's happiness (supposed equal in degree, with the proper allowance made for kind) counts for exactly as much as another's, that principle is a mere form of words with no rational meaning. Once those conditions are supplied, Bentham's dictum, "everybody to count for one, nobody for more than one," could be written under the principle of utility as an explanatory commentary.[D] Everybody's equal claim to happiness, in the estimation of the moralist and the legislator, involves an equal claim to all the means of happiness. The only exception is where the inevitable conditions of human life, and the general interest (which includes that of every individual), set limits to the maxim, and those limits ought to be strictly construed. Like every other maxim of justice, this one is by no means applied, or held applicable, universally. On the contrary, as I have already remarked, it bends to each person's ideas of social expediency. But wherever it is held to be applicable at all, it is held to be a dictate of justice. Everyone is deemed to have a _right_ to equality of treatment, unless some recognized social expediency requires the opposite. And so every social inequality that has stopped being considered expedient takes on the character not of simple inexpediency but of injustice. It looks so tyrannical that people are apt to wonder how it was ever tolerated. They forget that they themselves perhaps tolerate other inequalities, under an equally mistaken notion of expediency. Correcting these would make what they approve look as monstrous as what they have at last learned to condemn. The whole history of social improvement has been a series of transitions in which one custom or institution after another has ceased to be thought a primary necessity of social existence and has become a universally stigmatized injustice and tyranny. So it has been with the distinctions of slaves and freemen, nobles and serfs, patricians and plebeians. So it will be, and in part already is, with the aristocracies of color, race and sex.

What has been said shows that justice is a name for certain moral requirements which, taken together, stand higher in the scale of social utility, and so carry more paramount obligation, than any others. Still, particular cases may occur in which some other social duty is so important that it overrules one of the general maxims of justice. To save a life, for example, it may be not merely allowable but a duty to steal or seize by force the food or medicine needed, or to kidnap the only qualified medical practitioner and compel him to officiate. In such cases we do not call anything justice that is not a virtue. So we usually say, not that justice must give way to some other moral principle, but that what is just in ordinary cases is, because of that other principle, not just in the particular case. This useful accommodation of language keeps up the character of indefeasibility attributed to justice, and saves us from having to maintain that there can be laudable injustice.

The considerations now put forward resolve, I hold, the only real difficulty in the utilitarian theory of morals. It has always been evident that all cases of justice are also cases of expediency. The difference lies in the peculiar sentiment that attaches to the former and distinguishes it from the latter. Suppose this characteristic sentiment has been sufficiently accounted for. Suppose there is no need to assume any peculiarity of origin for it, and that it is simply the natural feeling of resentment, moralized by being made coextensive with the demands of social good. Suppose, further, that this feeling not only does but ought to exist in all the classes of cases to which the idea of justice corresponds. Then that idea no longer presents itself as a stumbling-block to the utilitarian ethics. Justice remains the proper name for certain social utilities that are vastly more important, and therefore more absolute and imperative, than any others are as a class (though not more so than others may be in particular cases). These utilities ought to be guarded, as they naturally are, by a sentiment that differs not only in degree but also in kind. It is distinguished from the milder feeling attached to the mere idea of promoting human pleasure or convenience, at once by the more definite nature of its commands and by the sterner character of its sanctions.

[Footnote D: Mr. Herbert Spencer (in his _Social Statics_) treats this implication of perfect impartiality between persons, found in the first principle of the utilitarian scheme, as a disproof of the claim of utility to be a sufficient guide to right. For, he says, the principle of utility presupposes the anterior principle that everybody has an equal right to happiness. A more correct description is that it supposes equal amounts of happiness to be equally desirable, whether felt by the same person or by different persons. This, however, is no presupposition and no premise needed to support the principle of utility. It is the very principle itself. For what is the principle of utility, if not that "happiness" and "desirable" are synonymous terms? If any anterior principle is implied, it can only be this: that the truths of arithmetic apply to the valuation of happiness, as to all other measurable quantities. [Mr. Herbert Spencer, in a private communication on the subject of the preceding Note, objects to being counted an opponent of Utilitarianism. He says that he regards happiness as the ultimate end of morality, but thinks that end only partly attainable by empirical generalizations from the observed results of conduct. In his view it is completely attainable only by deducing, from the laws of life and the conditions of existence, which kinds of action necessarily tend to produce happiness and which to produce unhappiness. Except for the word "necessarily," I have no dissent to express from this doctrine; and (leaving out that word) I do not know of any modern advocate of utilitarianism who holds a different opinion. Bentham, certainly, whom Mr. Spencer specifically meant in the _Social Statics_, is the last of writers to be charged with unwillingness to deduce the effect of actions on happiness from the laws of human nature and the universal conditions of human life. The usual charge against him is of relying too exclusively on such deductions, and refusing altogether to be bound by the generalizations from specific experience to which Mr. Spencer thinks utilitarians generally confine themselves. My own opinion (and, as I gather, Mr. Spencer's) is that in ethics, as in every other branch of scientific study, the consilience of the results of both these processes, each corroborating and verifying the other, is required to give any general proposition the kind and degree of evidence that amounts to scientific proof.]]
